To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 2 potential power analyses.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8’ to check the contents of 3 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: sample_size, alpha_level, effect_size, effect_size_metric, software

power_id power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
1 unknown other NA NA 0.80 0.68 other NA
2 posthoc other 115 NA 0.81 NA NA NA

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as ‘post-hoc’. Calculating observed power is almost never useful. If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

power_id text
1 To determine the sample size needed to achieve at least 80% statistical power under the interval testing framework, we conducted a simulation-based power analysis using pilot data (n = 52) from the unmatched-intensity condition [37]. All parameters and procedures described in the following section were specified a priori in our preregistration (see http://osf.io/sjvak). In pilot data, a machine learning classifier was able to predict whether the stimulus was a happy or angry face based on participants’ task performance, achieving a classification accuracy of 70%, with a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval (CI) of [67%, 73%]. Given that effect sizes derived from small samples are typically inflated [38] [39], we adopted a more conservative estimate of 68% (closer to the lower bound of the CI) for the true population accuracy and simulated 10,000 experiments, each drawing a random sample of participants ranging between 26 and 180, with each participant completing 190 trials of the visual search task (95 trials with happy faces and 95 with angry faces). The threshold for practical significance was set at 66%.
2 Results indicated that with 115 participants, corresponding to 4,370 trials in the test set, H 0 would be rejected in 81% of simulations, which corresponds to 81% statistical power for H 1 . The same sample size was targeted for the matched-intensity condition in the between-subject design.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 39 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .05 Specifically, traditional NHST can provide evidence against the null hypothesis (H 0 ) when p-values fall below a predetermined threshold (e.g., p < .05), but it cannot support H 0 when results are statistically non-significant.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (3)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 15 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the manuscript names a study (ex3) with no matching files in the repository; the repository separates out studies (ex1p, ex2p) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

What we found

  • We classified 1823 files: 1811 data, 8 code, 1 documentation, 3 materials.
  • We found 1206 tabular data files and extracted 2768 columns from 240 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 4 study groups (ex1, ex1p, ex2, ex2p), plus 1 collection-level file (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 966 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass local_path to point at a local copy. We ran automated data-quality checks on 2768 columns; 392 columns have at least one potential issue (196 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 196 columns whose name suggests personal information). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 2768 columns across 240 data files.

Issues Identified

392 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 240 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Each participant completed trials requiring the identification of angry and happy facial expressions (emotion is a within-subject factor), and was randomly assigned to one of two independent groups via separate recruitment links, corresponding to two distinct intensity conditions (between-subject factor): the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions.

In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants were presented with either angry or happy facial expressions at a maximum yet not-equalized level of intensity.

Two independent cohorts of participants were recruited via the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/) through separate study links, with the target population being native of the USA and the UK.

Participants were also excluded if they identified as neurodiverse, reported ongoing mental health conditions or treatment, were taking psychotropic medication, or reported having been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit disorder, or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

In total, 259 participants were recruited: 134 in the unmatched-intensity condition and 125 in the matched-intensity condition.

After all criteria were applied, 14 participants were excluded from the unmatched-intensity condition, necessitating the recruitment of 10 additional individuals to achieve the target sample size.

Upon reapplying all exclusion criteria to the entire updated sample, 119 participants remained eligible, from which a random subsample of 115 was extracted for analysis.

In the matched-intensity condition, 6 participants were excluded following the application of the accuracy-based criterion, yielding a final eligible sample of 119.

To familiarize participants with the task logic, a visual analogy was provided: participants were shown a reference blue square and asked to estimate its brightness on a 1-6 scale.

Analogously, participants were asked to treat the happy expression as a reference point along an imagined intensity continuum and to select the corresponding anger frame that best matched this perceived intensity.

After all participants completed this intensity-matching task, we calculated the mean frame selection across all participants to identify the matched-intensity angry stimulus for the experiment.

Upon accessing the study link, participants were first presented with a comprehensive overview of the experimental procedures, including detailed information on data confidentiality and security.

Only individuals who explicitly provided informed consent were allowed to proceed with the task.

To ensure consistency in stimulus presentation and response modality, participants were instructed to complete the experiment on a laptop or desktop computer.

On each trial, participants were presented with an array of eight grayscale photographs of facial expressions arranged in a circular layout (Fig. 1), with each face having the same eccentricity with respect to a central fixation point.

Participants were instructed to indicate, as quickly and accurately as possible, whether an emotional facial expression was present or absent in the set by pressing designated keys.

Participants were required to respond to every trial for the experiment to proceed.

The estimated duration of the task was approximately 30 minutes, and compensation was provided at a rate of $8/hour, in accordance with Prolific’s recommended payment guidelines.

Upon completing the task, participants were redirected to a debriefing page, which included a completion code to claim their compensation.

Recruitment was conducted using the “Include List” feature on the Prolific platform, which facilitated the precise identification and targeted re-invitation of eligible individuals.

The maximum data collection period was set at two weeks; however, data collection could conclude earlier if all eligible participants completed the task before the deadline.

As specified in the preregistration update, if fewer than 115 participants completed Study 2, additional participants with no prior involvement in any of our experiments would be recruited.

These new participants were asked to complete both the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions in that fixed order, separated by a washout period of at least two weeks.

No participants were excluded based on completion times below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR).

For this in-lab experiment we recruited a convenience sample of 16 participants (8 females; M age = 25 ± 3 years), who completed the standard visual search task involving angry and happy facial expressions across different experimental conditions.

Participants were adult Italian volunteers, recruited through local university channels and word-of-mouth.

After receiving a detailed explanation of the experimental procedures, all eligible participants provided written informed consent to take part in the study.

As in Study 1, participants were asked to perform an intensity-matching task through the designated web interface (see Fig. S1 in Supplementary Materials).

Trial types and spatial arrangements were randomized within each block.

Prior to the experimental task, participants completed the short form of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI-SF; [53]) to assess their dominant hand preference.

All participants were given a practice session of five trials to familiarize them with the procedure before starting the experiment.

Overall, each participant completed 200 trials (40 trials per 5 blocks), of which 80% contained one discrepant target and 20% did not.

Furthermore, participants were recruited online from the United States and the United Kingdom in Studies 1 and 2, and from Italy in Study 3, potentially limiting generalizability across cultural contexts.

No monetary compensation was offered, and participants were informed of their right to withdraw from the experiment at any time.

Ethics approval statement:

The current study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and received formal approval from the local Ethics Committee (Protocol No.

Study 2
In line with the original pre-registered study, the target sample size for Study 2 is 115 participants, each completing 250 trials of the matched-intensity condition (50 trials per block across 5 blocks).
sample_size_rationale We conducted a pilot experiment with 52 participants to test the feasibility of the task, refine procedures, and identify potential issues with stimulus presentation. This phase was essential to verify the viability of the two experimental conditions and enabled us to perform a subsequent power analysis to determine the appropriate sample size for the main study.
Participants were assigned to two balanced groups based on age, sex, autistic traits (i.e., AQ-10), social anxiety (i.e., LSAS), and trait anxiety (i.e., STAI-Y2). The first group (i.e., unmatched-intensity group, n = 26) was presented with either angry or happy facial expressions at a maximum yet not-equalized level of intensity between emotions, while the second group (i.e., matched-intensity group, n = 26) viewed stimuli at an intermediate yet equalized intensity.
Our experimental design is grounded in the principles of the Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), a framework that tests whether data provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis (H0) in favor of the alternative hypothesis (H1). While NHST can reject H0 when p-values fall below a predefined threshold (e.g., p<0.05), it does not provide direct support for H0 when results are non-significant. A non-significant result only tells us that we cannot reject the null hypothesis, leaving uncertainty about whether H0 is actually true or whether the study lacked statistical power to detect a pre-established effect. This limitation motivated us to incorporate interval testing, which enables conclusions about both H0 and H1. This approach involves the definition of an acceptance region for H0 by specifying the Smallest Effect Size Of Interest (SESOI). Then, one must evaluate whether the observed effect and its confidence interval lie within this region - supporting H0 - outside it - supporting H1, or crossing the H0 acceptance/rejection boundaries, resulting in an inconclusive test. This allows us to test both our hypotheses: the presence of a significant difference in the detection of angry vs. happy faces in the unmatched-intensity condition and the absence of such difference in the matched-intensity condition.
We implemented a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification model to assess whether reaction times (RTs) and response accuracy could reliably predict the facial expression (angry vs. happy) presented during the task (see “Statistical models” for detailed information) in left-out participants. To ensure our k-NN classifier was properly validated and tested, we used a 60%-20%-20% (train-validation-test) split for the nested cross-validation procedure.
We applied interval testing to the k-NN classification accuracy using a SESOI of 66%, which represents the minimum classification accuracy deemed practically significant for our purposes. If the lower boundary of the Confidence Interval (CI) of the model’s classification accuracy falls above the 66% - region of acceptance of H1 - we conclude that the behavioral features used as predictors are sufficiently discriminative of facial expressions of emotion. If, instead, the upper boundary of the CI falls below the 66% - region of acceptance of H0 - we support H0, indicating that the predictors lack significant predictive power. Last, the overlap between the CI and the SESOI threshold results in inconclusive findings.
We conducted a simulation-based power analysis using data from the unmatched-intensity condition to determine the sample size required to achieve 80% statistical power for the main study. More specifically, we simulated 10,000 replications of the experiment under the following parameters:
1. A population accuracy of 68%, representing a conservative estimate based on the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval achieved by the k-NN classifier trained on unmatched-intensity pilot data (mean accuracy: 70%, CI: [67%, 73%]).
2. A number of trials in the test between 988 and 6840 trials. Considering a total of 250 trials per participant, of which 190 valid trials including a non-neutral face, these observations correspond to a minimum of 26 and a maximum of 180 participants in the full sample.

We computed a 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the classification accuracy obtained from each simulation and assessed each time if the lower boundary of the accuracy CI exceeds the SESOI threshold. The statistical power of the experiment was then calculated as the proportion of simulations (i.e., experiments) in which H1 was supported. The decision criteria for evaluating hypotheses were as follows:
1. If the lower bound of the CI exceeds 66% (SESOI), we support H1 and conclude that the behavioral features used as predictors carry systematic and meaningful information that allows the k-NN classifier to well distinguish between angry and happy faces.
2. If the upper bound of the CI falls below 66%, we support H0, indicating that the behavioral features used as predictors lack sufficient discriminative power.
3. If the CI overlaps with the SESOI, the result is considered inconclusive, as the evidence is insufficient to support either hypothesis.

The power analysis confirmed that with a SESOI of 66%, a population effect size of 68%, and a width of the CI of 95%, 4370 trials are needed in the test set to detect an effect with 80% power. Given that each participant contributes 190 trials, this corresponds to 23 participants allocated to the test set (20% of the total dataset), resulting in a total sample of 115 participants per group.

Study 2
In order to replicate the absence of the happy face advantage in the matched-intensity condition, we will recruit a sample equal in size to that of the original pre-registered study.
measured_variables The main measured variables are speed and accuracy in the detection of either angry or happy facial expressions in a visual search task:
1. Speed is operationalized as reaction times (RTs) measured in milliseconds (ms). RTs are recorded for each single trial starting from the onset of the stimulus (i.e., the display of the array of facial expressions) until the participant’s response.
2. Accuracy refers to whether participants correctly classify the presence or absence of an emotionally discrepant facial expression (angry or happy) in each trial.

Study 2
Consistent with the original pre-registered study, Study 2 will include the collection and analysis of both reaction times and detection accuracy.
statistical_tests We will develop a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification model to test whether emotional categories could be predicted based on participants’ task performance. More specifically, the target variable will be the emotion being presented (angry vs. happy), while the predictors will include detection speed (operationalized as RTs) and detection accuracy. The model’s classification performance will reflect the discriminative value of the input features.
The k-NN model will be evaluated using a nested cross-validation procedure to ensure robust generalization and optimal parameter selection. In the inner loop (train-validation split), a 4-fold cross-validation will be performed to identify the optimal number of neighbors by minimizing classification error in the validation set. In the outer loop (train-test split), a 5-fold cross-validation will be used to assess the model’s performance on unseen test data.
Classification accuracy will serve as the primary performance metric, and a bootstrapped 95% Confidence Interval (CI) will be calculated to quantify the variability of the model’s predictions.
We will apply interval testing to the k-NN classification accuracy using a SESOI of 66%. This threshold will represent the minimum classification accuracy deemed practically significant for our purposes. If the classification accuracy CI falls entirely above 66%, we will conclude that the model demonstrated significant accuracy in discriminating emotions, supporting H1. Conversely, if the classification accuracy CI falls entirely below 66%, we will accept H0, indicating that the predictors lacked sufficient ability to differentiate between angry and happy faces. Results where the CI overlaps the SESOI will be deemed inconclusive.

Study 2
For Study 2, we will replicate the analysis pipeline used in the original pre-registered study. Specifically, the same code and functions uploaded to the OSF project repository (https://osf.io/vhcyt/) prior to this pre-registration update will be applied to the Study 2 dataset, ensuring consistency in all analyses across both studies. This includes variable transformations, inference criteria, data exclusion rules, treatment of missing data, and exploratory analyses.
research_questions We hypothesize that the detection advantage for certain facial expressions, such as happiness or anger, observed in the literature is primarily driven by low-level perceptual features rather than the emotional content of the expressions. Accordingly, we propose and test two hypotheses:
1. In the unmatched-intensity condition, where happy and angry facial expressions are presented at their maximum – unequalized – intensity, happy faces will be detected faster and more accurately than angry faces. This directional hypothesis is grounded in prior research indicating that specific perceptual features, such as the saliency of a conspicuous smile in happy facial expressions, facilitate their detection (Calvo & Nummenmaa, 2008).
2. In the matched-intensity condition, where the intensity of happy and angry facial expressions is equalized, we hypothesize the detection advantage for happy faces will no longer be present. This hypothesis reflects the expectation that balancing the perceptual low-level features of the stimuli will mitigate the detection bias observed in the unmatched-intensity condition.
study_type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
blinding For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
randomization Each participant will be asked to complete a total of 250 trials divided into 5 blocks (50 trials/block). Within each block, randomization will occur at multiple levels:
1. Trial level. Trials from each trial type (i.e., including only neutral faces, with one angry face target, and with one happy face target) will appear in a random order.
2. Stimulus location level. Faces will appear in eight possible locations, arranged in a circle, with equal eccentricity with respect to the central fixation point. The order in which stimuli will appear in each location will be randomized. However, to control for a potential positional bias, we will ensure that both emotional facial expressions of the same actor will be displayed in the same location within each block. In other words, if an actor’s angry face is shown in Location 3, the happy face of the same actor will also appear in Location 3, within the same block.
existing_data Registration prior to creation of data
existing_data_explanation For detailed information regarding the pilot experiment and the subsequent power calculation to determine the sample size for the current study, please refer to the “Sample size rationale” section.
manipulated_variables We manipulated the intensity of angry and happy facial expressions presented to participants across the two experimental conditions:
1. In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants will be presented with frames extracted from ADFES’ videos depicting anger and happiness at maximum intensity. For each frame of the video sequences, the displacement field that aligns two temporally consecutive 2-D images has been estimated using the “imregdemons” function in MATLAB. This is a necessary step to identify the frame with the highest displacement value, which corresponds to the expression’s peak intensity.
2. In the matched-intensity condition, both angry and happy faces will be presented at an intermediate but equalized intensity level. This process followed a two-step procedure:
2.1 Step 1: Video clips depicting happiness were manually inspected to identify the frame immediately preceding the exposure of teeth. This step aims to minimize visual confounds, such as exposed teeth in conspicuous smiles, which may result in a “blob” of high local luminance and heightened local contrast around the mouth region.
2.2 Step 2: An independent cohort of subjects reviewed all frames from video clips of anger by the same actor/actress and selected the one they judged to match the intensity of the preselected happy expression most closely. The average frames selected by this cohort were designated as the angry stimuli for the matched-intensity condition. This methodology helps ensure that stimuli from both emotional categories are presented at the same intensity levels, thereby balancing their perceptual features.
Lastly, both sets of stimuli underwent the same preprocessing steps: non-facial areas (e.g., hair, neck) were removed using an ellipsoidal mask, and low-level image properties were standardized by converting the images to grayscale and normalizing luminance and spatial frequency using the SHINE Toolbox in MATLAB.
transformations For the k-NN classification model, reaction times will be centered within participants using MATLAB’s “normalize” function with the “center” option. This process involves subtracting each participant’s average RT from their individual RT values, thereby adjusting for baseline differences in overall response speed while preserving the original variability. No further recoding will be required for the k-NN analysis.
inference_criteria We will develop a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification model to assess the detection of angry vs. happy facial expressions. In a interval testing framework, inferences will be based on the bootstrapped 95% Confidence Interval (CI) of the model’s classification accuracy, which will be compared to the Smallest Effect Size Of Interest (SESOI) threshold:
1. If the CI of the classification accuracy falls entirely above the SESOI threshold - region of acceptance of H1 - we will conclude there is evidence supporting the existence of a significant difference in detection between angry and happy expressions (support for H1).
2. If the CI falls entirely below the SESOI threshold - region of acceptance of H0 - we will interpret this as evidence supporting the absence of a significant difference between emotions in detection (support for H0).
3. If the CI overlaps with the SESOI threshold, the results will be deemed inconclusive, suggesting that the data do not provide clear evidence for either hypothesis.
data_exclusion_criteria Data exclusion will be based on the following criteria:
1. Participant-level
1.1 Exclusion based on overall completion time of the experiment
Participants with exceptionally short completion times will be excluded from the analysis. Specifically, we will calculate the interquartile range (IQR) of the total task completion times and exclude those whose times fall below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5×IQR. Here, Q1 represents the 25th percentile of the completion times distribution. Such unusually short durations may indicate that the participant rushed through the task, potentially compromising data quality by not engaging adequately or responding without sufficient consideration.
1.2 Exclusion based on accuracy rates
Participants with exceptionally low accuracy rates will be excluded from the analysis. Accuracy rates will be assessed separately for each emotion category, and participants whose accuracy rates fall below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5×IQR in either emotion category will be excluded. This approach aims to mitigate potential issues such as lack of understanding of the task, inattentiveness, or random responding. Importantly, no upper threshold for accuracy will be applied, as participants with high accuracy rates are assumed to have completed the task as intended.
2 Single trial-level
2.1 Exclusion of single trials based on reaction times (RTs)
Trials with unusually long reaction times (RTs) will be excluded from the analysis, as they may reflect instances of distraction or disengagement from the task. Specifically, we will calculate the IQR of the RTs distribution and exclude trials with RTs exceeding the third quartile (Q3, or 75th percentile) plus 1.5×IQR. This threshold is selected to eliminate extreme outliers while preserving the integrity of the majority of the data.
missing_data_handling Responses are mandatory for each trial to proceed, guaranteeing that data are collected for all 250 trials per participant. As a result, we do not anticipate missing data at the participant level. Participants who do not complete all trials will be excluded from the analysis. In the event that single trials will present missing data due to technical issues (e.g., server errors, interruptions during data recording), those specific trials will be excluded from the analysis.
exploratory_analyses As the sample size was determined based on a power calculation for the k-NN classification model, this model will serve as the primary method for statistical inference. However, in addition to the main analysis, we will conduct exploratory analyses using Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects models (GLMMs) to examine the effects of emotion (angry vs. happy) and condition (unmatched vs. matched intensity) on detection speed and accuracy:
1. Reaction times (RTs) will be analyzed using a GLMM with an inverse Gaussian distribution and a log link function, as RT distributions are typically positively skewed and deviate from normality. The model will include emotion (angry vs. happy), condition (unmatched vs matched intensity) and their interaction as fixed effects, while participant ID and actor ID will be incorporated as random intercepts to account for potential individual differences in baseline response times, as well as variability in the ease with which different stimuli are detected. Based on our hypotheses, we anticipate a significant Emotion × Condition interaction, indicating that the effect of emotion on detection speed varies significantly between the two conditions. Specifically, we predict that in the unmatched-intensity condition, happy faces will be detected faster than angry faces due to the unbalanced saliency of their perceptual features. In contrast, this advantage is expected to diminish or disappear in the matched-intensity condition, where the intensity of expressions is equalized.
2. Accuracy will be analyzed using a separate GLMM with a binomial distribution and a logit link function, given that the outcome variable consists of binary responses (correct vs. incorrect). The fixed effects and random intercepts will mirror those in the RT analysis, ensuring consistency in our approach. We expect accuracy results to follow a similar pattern to RTs, with a significant Emotion × Condition interaction reflecting a detection advantage for happy faces in the unmatched condition compared to the matched condition.
For both models, statistical significance will be assessed using a conventional threshold of p < 0.05.
study_design_overview The current study aims to compare participants’ performance in a visual search task for angry and happy facial expressions across different experimental conditions. More specifically, all participants are presented with arrays of eight photographs of actors, extracted from a validated database (van der Schalk et al. 2011). They will be instructed to detect the emotionally discrepant expression - either angry or happy - among neutral distractors and press a designated button on the keyboard as quickly and accurately as possible.
Full-blown expressions at their maximum intensity will be presented in the first condition (i.e., unmatched-intensity condition). Conversely, in the second condition (i.e., matched-intensity condition), happy and angry facial expressions will be equivalent in perceived intensity, as determined by an independent cohort of participants (please see “Manipulated variables” for more information). This matching process seeks to prevent one expression from being more perceptually salient than the other. The purpose of this manipulation is to examine whether the detection advantage expected in the unmatched-intensity condition persists when intensity-based perceptual differences are controlled for.
In both conditions, visual search performances are evaluated based on response accuracy (i.e., correct detection of the presence/absence of an emotional face) and reaction times from the onset of the stimulus display until the participant’s button press. By comparing participants’ performances toward happy and angry faces across conditions, we will unveil whether and to what extent low-level features, rather than emotion category, determine any advantage in the detection of emotional facial expressions.
To this purpose, we build a mixed experimental design with two factors:
1. Intensity matching is a between-subjects factor. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups:
- The first group is presented with facial expressions of anger and happiness at their maximum intensity, where the unbalanced perceptual saliency of features is retained (e.g., happy faces may display higher local luminance in the mouth region due to teeth exposure in conspicuous smiles).
- The second group is presented with the same facial expressions, but at an intermediate yet equalized intensity, ensuring that low-level features are balanced across emotions.
2. Emotion is a within-subjects factor. Participants are presented with arrays of neutral facial expressions, within which one face may display either an angry or a happy expression.
The presentation order of arrays is randomized across participants and experimental sessions to prevent potential biases due to learning or sequence effects. Each block of the experiment will consist of three trial types presented in a randomized order:
- All faces in the array display a neutral expression
- One emotionally discrepant angry face appears among the neutral faces
- One emotionally discrepant happy face appears among the neutral faces.

Study 2
The present study is designed as a replication of the absence of a happy face advantage observed in the originally pre-registered matched-intensity condition. For this replication attempt, the same group of individuals who previously participated in the unmatched-intensity condition—where angry and happy faces were displayed at their maximum, unequalized intensity—will be re-invited to complete the matched-intensity condition. In line with the original study design, in Study 2, facial expressions in the matched-intensity condition will be presented at an intermediate, intensity-equalized level between emotions.
Recruitment for Study 2 will be conducted via the “Include List” feature on the Prolific platform, ensuring that only participants who completed the initial unmatched-intensity condition will be eligible for re-testing.
To mitigate potential carryover effects from prior exposure, a washout period of at least two weeks will be implemented between the two sessions. As in the original pre-registered study, stimuli will be presented in randomized order to minimize sequence effects and avoid systematic biases. The task structure and instructions will remain identical across sessions; the only manipulation will concern the intensity level of the emotional expressions to which participants are exposed. Importantly, they will not be informed about this manipulation.
The order of condition exposure is fixed: all participants will have previously completed the unmatched-intensity task and will subsequently be invited to complete the matched-intensity task.
For an illustration of the study design, please refer to: https://osf.io/n47cv.
data_collection_procedures Participants will be recruited via the online Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/), with a target population being native of the USA and the UK. A total of 250 participants (125 per condition) will be recruited, aiming for a final sample of 115 eligible participants per group. The two groups are as follows:
1. Unmatched-intensity group: participants (n = 125 recruited, 115 final sample) will be shown angry and happy faces at their maximum, unbalanced intensity.
2. Matched-intensity group: participants (n = 125 recruited, 115 final sample) will be shown angry and happy faces at an equalized, intermediate, intensity.
Two separate recruitment links will be generated, each designated for a specific experimental group. Recruitment settings on Prolific will ensure that participants who completed the first condition are excluded from participating in the second condition.
Participants are deemed eligible if they meet the following inclusion criteria.
Inclusion criteria:
1. Participants must be at least 18 years old.
2. Participants must have normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
3. Participants must be native English speakers.
They will be excluded if:
1. They have a self-reported history of mental illness.
2. They have a self-reported history of language-related disorders.
3. They identify/have been diagnosed as neurodiverse.
4. They have received a diagnosis of dyslexia.
5. They report a history of head injury.
6. They have a self-reported mental health illness or condition or are undergoing mental health treatment.
7. They are currently taking psychotropic medication.
8. They have received a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
9. They have received a diagnosis of attention deficit disorder (ADD) or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
10. Participants who have previously participated in one of our conditions.
Upon accessing the study link, participants will provide informed consent after being presented with a comprehensive description of the experimental procedures and the security measures protecting their data. In detail, this study has been approved by the local Ethical Committee under protocol number 12/2022 (i.e., “Comitato Etico Congiunto per la ricerca della Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna e della Scuola Normale Superiore”) and will be conducted in compliance with current data protection laws, including D. Lgs 196/2003 and EU GDPR 679/2016. All data will be collected anonymously, and no identifying information will be linked to individual responses. The collected data will be used exclusively for statistical purposes. Participants will have the right to withdraw from the study at any time by simply closing the webpage, and no consequences will derive from that.
The task will be implemented using jsPsych, an open-source JavaScript library, ensuring precise stimulus presentation and accurate data collection (de Leeuw, 2015). The short form of the “Edinburgh Handedness Inventory” (EHI) will be administered to participants before starting the experimental task to assess their dominant hand and account for potential variability in task performance related to handedness. The task must be completed exclusively on a laptop.
Upon completing all five blocks, they will receive compensation of £8/hour, in line with Prolific recommended rates for the estimated time to complete the experiment (approximately 30 minutes). Compensation is contingent upon the successful completion of the task. Afterward, participants will be directed to a debriefing page to save their Prolific completion code and be thanked for their participation.
The experiment consists of five blocks, each containing 50 trials, during which participants will be presented with arrays of eight faces. Throughout the experiment, the online platform will automatically collect data on two key metrics: reaction times and accuracy. Reaction times will be measured as the time taken from the moment the stimulus appears on the screen until the participant makes their response. Accuracy will be computed as the participant’s correct identification of the presence/absence of an emotional facial expression among neutral distractors. Data will be logged for each trial.
Participants will also be monitored for completion time to verify that the duration of the experiment aligns with expected time ranges. Here, completion time refers to the total amount of time elapsed from when a participant clicks on the study link to when they submit their final response and are redirected to the debriefing page. Any participant who completes the task too quickly (i.e., the first quartile minus 1.5×IQR, but please see “Data exclusion” for detailed information) will have their data excluded from the final analysis.

Study Timeline:
1. Preparation (3 weeks)
1.1 Experiment Setup
1.1.1 Develop the experiment using JsPsych, ensuring that all aspects of the design, including randomization and stimulus presentation, function as intended.
1.1.2 Create two separate experiment links for the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions, differing only in the intensity of the stimuli participants will be shown.
1.1.3 Test the links to confirm they are error-free and ready for deployment.
1.2 Screening and Pilot Testing
1.2.1 Use Prolific screening settings to ensure only participants meeting the inclusion criteria can access the study.
1.2.2 Identify eligible participants and conduct a small-scale pilot test (i.e., 25 participants per group) to identify any technical, timing, or task-related issues. Pilot data will not be included in final analyses.
1.2.3 Collect, review, and analyze pilot data. Refine the task and address any issues (e.g., unclear instructions, overly long/short durations, or problematic stimuli) if needed.
1.2.4 Incorporate feedback from the pilot test and finalize the experiment.

At the time of this pre-registration submission, all the previously mentioned steps had already been completed.

2. Recruitment & data collection (3 weeks)
2.1 Publish the link for the unmatched-intensity condition on the Prolific platform.
2.2 Recruit 125 participants and actively monitor progress to ensure completion rates are on track and data integrity is maintained.
2.3 Once data for 125 participants is successfully collected, we will launch the matched-intensity condition link.
2.4 Publish the link for the matched-intensity condition on the Prolific platform, ensuring the recruitment of an independent cohort of 125 participants. Prolific screening settings will automatically exclude individuals who took part in the unmatched-intensity experiment.
2.5 Actively monitor data collection for the matched-intensity group to ensure smooth progress and data quality.
3 Data analysis (2 weeks)
3.1 Exclude participants who completed the task in an unusually short time.
3.2 Check for missing data across both groups.
3.3 Check whether at least 115 participants per group have provided usable data. If we collect more data than expected based on estimated dropout, we will randomly select 115 participants from the larger sample of those providing usable data. Conversely, if we collect less data than originally planned according to power calculations, we will continue the recruitment phase until 115 participants with usable data are included in the final sample.
3.4 Perform statistical analyses.
4. Final reporting & dissemination (4 weeks)
4.1 Prepare the final study report, summarizing the key statistical findings.
4.2 Publish or share the findings as appropriate.

Study 2
To replicate the absence of a happy face advantage observed in the matched-intensity condition of the pre-registered study, only participants who previously completed the unmatched-intensity condition will be recruited. Recruitment will be conducted via the “Include List” feature on the Prolific platform, which allows for precise targeting of individuals who meet specific eligibility criteria—in this case, prior participation in the unmatched-intensity condition and the provision of usable data (see the Data Exclusion section of the original pre-registration for details). This group consists of 119 individuals.
Participants will receive the same compensation as in the original pre-registered study.
Data collection for Study 2 will begin at least two weeks after the completion of the unmatched-intensity condition. This washout period is intended to reduce potential carryover effects. The maximum duration for data collection is set at two weeks but may end earlier if all eligible participants complete the study before the deadline.
If fewer than the targeted 115 participants will provide usable data in Study 2, additional individuals who have not participated in any previous experiments will be recruited. These new participants will complete both the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity sessions, in that fixed order, with a washout period of at least two weeks between sessions.

Below, we describe some best coding practices and give the results of automatic evaluation of these practices in the code files below. This check may miss things or produce false positives if your scripts are less typical.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). None of the files found could be checked for comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

No packages/libraries were detected as loaded in the code files. (This check reads R and Python imports; other languages are not scanned for packages.) Even when no imports are detected, it is good practice to record the exact package versions the analysis depended on — see “Reproducible Environment” below.

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

Reproducibility Check

MATLAB code, no reproducible output

8 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run diary('output.txt') (or diary on) before the analysis and diary off after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use publish('script.m', 'pdf') (or the Live Editor’s Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break.
