The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Humans are assumed to prioritize facial expressions because of the evolutionary significance of their affective content. Here, we show that this assumption does not survive rigorous control of perceptual structure. Across three studies integrating preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial expressions, and eye-tracking data, and combining frequentist interval testing with a predefined smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses, we tested whether detection advantages for happy and angry faces are better explained by the perceptual distinctiveness of stimuli than by their affective content. Behavioral and oculomotor measures reliably predicted emotion category when expressions were presented at full, perceptually unbalanced, intensity. By contrast, when expression intensity was matched, both interval testing and Bayesian ROPE analyses supported the absence of a practically meaningful effect. In addition, detection speed and accuracy were best explained by geometric deviation from a neutral face, independent of emotional category. These findings indicate that apparent emotion advantages in visual search arise from the perceptual characteristics of facial expressions rather than from privileged access to emotional meaning, challenging evolutionary accounts of attentional prioritization.

Introduction

Humans are social beings whose successful functioning depends on efficiently interpreting others' mental states and preparing appropriate responses [1]. Because attentional resources are limited, perceptual systems are thought to prioritize cues that signal affective and socially relevant information over competing input. From an evolutionary perspective, such prioritization is assumed to confer adaptive advantages by facilitating rapid responses to emotionally significant stimuli [2, 3].

Although facial expressions do not map one-to-one onto subjective emotional experience [4], the human face remains a powerful tool to signal social intentions. Smiles, for example, often signal affiliation, whereas baring the teeth can signal threat [5]. Consistent with their social relevance, numerous studies report facilitated detection of emotional relative to neutral faces (e.g., [6] [7] [8]), an effect commonly interpreted as reflecting adaptive prioritization. Importantly, this attentional preference has been observed even when emotional expressions were irrelevant to the task, for example with both happy and angry faces attracting the gaze during visual search even though the target was defined by gender [9]. This raises a critical question: Are all facial expressions prioritized equally, or do specific expressions, such as threat-related versus affiliative signals, receive preferential access to attention? One influential account holds that stimuli signaling potential threat receive prioritized access to attentional resources because their rapid detection supports timely fight-or-flight responses (the threat-advantage hypothesis; [10, 11]). This view predicts the "face-in-the-crowd" effect: Angry faces should be detected more efficiently than non-threatening faces because of their hostile value. Empirical support for this claim largely comes from visual search studies reporting faster and more accurate detection of angry faces among neutral distractors [12] [13] [14], with performance interpreted as a proxy for emotion-driven attentional prioritization.

Subsequent work challenged the threat-advantage account by showing that prioritization effects for angry faces were confounded by low-level visual properties of the stimuli [15]. In response, researchers adopted schematic faces, which allow geometric features to be manipulated while ostensibly controlling low-level visual characteristics. Although detection advantages for negatively valenced expressions were frequently replicated using such stimuli [13, 16], their interpretation proved inconsistent, as schematic features often failed to map onto specific emotional categories [12, 17]. More strikingly, Horstmann and colleagues [18] demonstrated that modifying the geometry of the facial outline could reverse the direction of the search asymmetry without substantially altering the perceived emotional valence of the faces. In addition, other studies failed to replicate an anger superiority effect (ASE [10]; e.g., [15, 19]), and have often reported the existence of a happiness superiority effect (HSE; [20]). In HSE, happy faces are detected more rapidly and accurately than angry or fearful faces among neutral distractors [8, [21] [22], an advantage that is especially pronounced when photographic images of real faces are used [23]. However, both ASE and HSE have been reported with photographic faces depending on the stimulus set employed [24], and subsequent work has shown that changing even a few facial identities within the same database can reverse the direction of the reaction-time advantage [25].

Öhman and coauthors [26] likewise demonstrated that distractor redundancy and target gender affected the relative prioritization of angry versus happy faces, with an anger superiority effect emerging specifically for male targets among redundant distractors.

Given the inconsistent pattern of detection advantages observed across studies, it is reasonable to question whether these effects reflect emotion at all. An alternative explanation comes from computational models of visual salience, which propose that selective attention can be guided by local variations in basic image properties, such as luminance, contrast and edge orientation [27] [28]. Applied to facial expressions, this account suggests that detection advantages may arise from the perceptual distinctiveness of specific facial features rather than from their emotional meaning [29]. For instance, Horstmann and colleagues [30] demonstrated that mouth opening and the accompanying visibility of teeth may facilitate visual search for both happy and angry faces, potentially producing a superiority effect for either expression. The contribution of such features has also been investigated by disrupting normal face processing through scrambling or inversion, while leaving local visual information available. Search efficiency remained largely unaffected by face inversion [31] and both anger and happiness superiority effects were observed in this context [32].

Building on this literature, we conducted a rigorous comparison of ASE and HSE by systematically varying the degree of perceptual distinctiveness between angry and happy photographic faces to test whether detection advantages for either emotion persist once expressionrelated perceptual differences are minimized. To this aim, we extracted static frames from dynamic facial expressions of happiness and anger [33] at two intensity levels: a maximal, perceptually unmatched, intensity and an intermediate, perceptually matched, intensity. Participants performed a visual search task in which they identified a single happy or angry face among neutral distractors.

This manipulation allowed us to test whether shorter detection times and higher accuracy for one emotion persist when lower-level perceptual structure is controlled.

If detection advantages reflect privileged access to affective meaning, a consistent advantage for specific expressions should emerge in both matched and unmatched conditions. Conversely, if attentional prioritization is driven by the perceptual characteristics of the stimuli, an advantage should arise only when expressions differ in these characteristics and should disappear once intensity and magnitude of facial displacement are equated between emotions. We tested these competing predictions across three studies combining preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial stimuli, and eye-tracking data to assess both detection performance and attentional dynamics. We then used interval testing and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses to formally assess competing hypotheses (i.e., presence or absence of an emotion-driven performance advantage).

Results converged on a perceptual account: detection performance differed between emotions only under the perceptually unmatched condition, where affective meaning covaried with perceptual distinctiveness. This asymmetry disappeared when perceptual features were matched across emotion categories, thereby dissociating emotion from differences in stimulus appearance.

Oculomotor behavior likewise varied more between emotions in the unmatched than in the matched condition, both in the time taken to first look at a face (time to first fixation) and the total time spent looking at it (dwell time), suggesting a faster visual search only when perceptual distinctiveness is maximal. Last, behavioral performance correlated with the geometric displacement of the emotional facial expressions from neutrality.

Study 1 Methods

Experimental design

A 2×2 mixed-design experimental paradigm was employed to examine participants' performance in a visual search task involving the detection of emotional facial expressions. Each participant completed trials requiring the identification of angry and happy facial expressions (emotion is a within-subject factor), and was randomly assigned to one of two independent groups via separate recruitment links, corresponding to two distinct intensity conditions (between-subject factor): the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions. In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants were presented with either angry or happy facial expressions at a maximum yet not-equalized level of intensity. Within this context, we anticipated a detection advantage for happy faces, grounded in existing literature suggesting that in photographic stimuli uncorrected low-level visual features (most notably, the pronounced luminance and contrast associated with a conspicuous, tooth-exposing smile) may enhance perceptual distinctiveness and facilitate detection [34]. In the present study, we use the term "perceptual distinctiveness" to refer to the visual characteristics of facial expressions that influence their detection during visual search. These characteristics can affect performance through the interplay of bottom-up (e.g., feature contrast) and top-down mechanisms (e.g., goal-directed attentional guidance).

By contrast, the matched-intensity condition employed stimuli at an intermediate level of intensity, perceptually-equalized across emotions to minimize differences in low-level visual features (see Stimulus selection and perceptual matching for details). We hypothesized that correcting for such perceptual confounds would eliminate the detection bias observed in the unmatched-intensity condition.

In both conditions, visual search performance was assessed through two behavioral metrics: response accuracy (i.e., correct identification of the presence or absence of an emotional target among neutral distractors) and reaction time (i.e., latency between stimulus onset to keypress response).

Sample size justification

Our study intended to test two complementary hypotheses: first, that a practical and statistical difference exists in the detection of happy versus angry faces when stimuli are unbalanced in terms of low-level visual features (i.e., the unmatched-intensity condition); and second, that such a practical and statistical difference would no longer be observed when perceptual features are matched between emotions (i.e., the matched-intensity condition).

Demonstrating both the presence and absence of an effect necessitates an analytical approach capable of supporting inferences in both directions. Conventional Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) is not suitable for this purpose [35]. Specifically, traditional NHST can provide evidence against the null hypothesis (H 0 ) when p-values fall below a predetermined threshold (e.g., p < .05), but it cannot support H 0 when results are statistically non-significant.

To overcome this limitation, we adopted an interval testing approach, which enables inferences about the presence or the absence of an effect by comparing the observed statistics and its 95% confidence interval to a predefined threshold of practical significance [36]. This threshold, known as the Smallest Effect Size of Interest or SESOI, represents the minimum effect size deemed practical for interpretation. If the entire 95% confidence interval (CI) lies above the SESOI threshold, the result is interpreted as supportive of the alternative hypothesis (H 1 ), indicating a practically meaningful effect. Conversely, if the CI lies entirely below the SESOI, the result supports the null hypothesis (H 0 ), suggesting the absence of such an effect. If the CI overlaps the SESOI, the result is considered inconclusive.

To determine the sample size needed to achieve at least 80% statistical power under the interval testing framework, we conducted a simulation-based power analysis using pilot data (n = 52) from the unmatched-intensity condition [37]. All parameters and procedures described in the following section were specified a priori in our preregistration (see http://osf.io/sjvak). In pilot data, a machine learning classifier was able to predict whether the stimulus was a happy or angry face based on participants' task performance, achieving a classification accuracy of 70%, with a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval (CI) of [67%, 73%]. Given that effect sizes derived from small samples are typically inflated [38] [39], we adopted a more conservative estimate of 68% (closer to the lower bound of the CI) for the true population accuracy and simulated 10,000 experiments, each drawing a random sample of participants ranging between 26 and 180, with each participant completing 190 trials of the visual search task (95 trials with happy faces and 95 with angry faces). The threshold for practical significance was set at 66%.

Because model performance would be evaluated using a 60%-20%-20% train-validationtest split to obtain an unbiased estimate of cross-validated accuracy, the number of trials in the test set ranged from 988 (n = 26) to 6,840 (n = 180). For each simulated test set, we calculated the 95% confidence interval of classification accuracy and interpreted the outcome as supporting H 1 , H 0 , or inconclusive result, depending on whether the interval lay entirely above, entirely below, or overlapped the SESOI, respectively.

Results indicated that with 115 participants, corresponding to 4,370 trials in the test set, H 0 would be rejected in 81% of simulations, which corresponds to 81% statistical power for H 1 . The same sample size was targeted for the matched-intensity condition in the between-subject design.

Participants

Two independent cohorts of participants were recruited via the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/) through separate study links, with the target population being native of the USA and the UK. Recruitment settings were configured to ensure that participants who completed one condition were excluded from participating in the other, thereby maintaining the independence of the two groups. The current study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and received formal approval from the local Ethics Committee (Protocol No. 12/2022, "Comitato Etico Congiunto per la ricerca della Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna e della Scuola Normale Superiore"). All data were collected anonymously and handled in strict accordance with current data protection legislation, including the Italian Legislative Decree 196/2003 and the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR 679/2016). No personally identifiable information was gathered, and the data were used exclusively for scientific and statistical purposes. All participants retained the right to withdraw from the study at any time without any consequences by simply closing the browser window.

Exclusion criteria included self-reported history of mental illness, language-related disorders, or head injury. Participants were also excluded if they identified as neurodiverse, reported ongoing mental health conditions or treatment, were taking psychotropic medication, or reported having been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit disorder, or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. In total, 259 participants were recruited: 134 in the unmatched-intensity condition and 125 in the matched-intensity condition. To account for potential participant exclusion based on our preregistered criteria (see OSF Registration, Data Exclusion section), we intentionally over-recruited beyond the minimum required sample size, ensuring that each condition retained a sufficiently powered sample of 115 participants after data cleaning. Recruitment was initially capped at 250 participants (125 per group). If more than 115 eligible participants per group provided usable data, a random subsample of 115 was selected; if fewer met the criteria, recruitment was extended until the target sample size was reached.

Data were excluded based on two levels: participant and trial. At the participant level, we evaluated total task completion time and response accuracy. Here, completion time refers to the total amount of time elapsed from when a participant clicks on the study link to when they submit their final response and are redirected to the debriefing page (see Experimental procedure for details). Participants with completion times falling below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) were flagged for exclusion, as short durations may indicate insufficient engagement with the task. However, no participants met this criterion. Accuracy-based exclusions were applied separately for each emotion category. Participants whose accuracy scores in either category fell below Q1 -1.5 × IQR were excluded to minimize the impact of random responding, inattentiveness, or misunderstanding of task instructions. No upper threshold was set for accuracy, as high performance was interpreted as evidence of appropriate task engagement. At the single-trial level, exclusions were based on reaction times (RTs). Trials with RTs exceeding the third quartile (Q3) plus 1.5 × IQR were removed, as excessively long latencies may reflect distraction or disengagement.

After all criteria were applied, 14 participants were excluded from the unmatched-intensity condition, necessitating the recruitment of 10 additional individuals to achieve the target sample size. Upon reapplying all exclusion criteria to the entire updated sample, 119 participants remained eligible, from which a random subsample of 115 was extracted for analysis. At the trial level, 1,110 trials were excluded due to excessively long response times.

In the matched-intensity condition, 6 participants were excluded following the application of the accuracy-based criterion, yielding a final eligible sample of 119. As this number met the pre-specified minimal threshold, no further recruitment was required. A random subsample of 115 participants was again selected for analysis, and 1,320 trials were excluded on the basis of delayed response times.

Stimulus selection and perceptual matching

Unlike many facial expression datasets that rely on static or artificially generated stimuli, we constructed our stimulus set using the "Amsterdam Dynamic Facial Expression Set" (ADFES), a validated database comprising 648 dynamic emotional expressions performed by 22 professional actors (10 female, 12 male) from diverse ethnic backgrounds. The use of real actors is essential for eliciting affective responses in viewers [40]. ADFES includes portrayals of nine discrete emotions: the six Ekman's basic ones (anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise) alongside contempt, pride and embarrassment. Each video has a duration of approximately 6 to 6.5 seconds, beginning with a 500-millisecond neutral baseline, followed by the onset of the expression, and culminating in a 5-second apex phase. Emotional expressions were generated using standardized configurations of facial Action Units (AUs), incorporating the most characteristic features outlined by Ekman and Friesen [41], Keltner [42], and Tracy & Robins [43]. The ADFES stimuli have been extensively validated and received excellent recognition rates [33].

For the purposes of this study, only video clips depicting anger and happiness were selected. To identify peak-intensity frames for the unmatched-intensity condition, we computed the displacement fields aligning two temporally consecutive frames from each video sequence using the imregdemons function in MATLAB [44]. This image registration technique enabled us to detect the frame with the highest value of framewise displacement, which corresponds to the apex of the expression. The procedure was applied to both happy and angry clips for a selected subset of actors (n = 19). These selected frames served as experimental stimuli in the unmatchedintensity condition.

We assessed the perceptual validity of this displacement-based selection by collecting independent intensity judgments from human scorers (n = 9; 6 females, M age = 33 ± 7 years) and comparing their choices with the frames identified by the registration algorithm. In this validation task, participants viewed all frames from the anger and happiness sequences and, for each actor, selected the frame they perceived as displaying the highest level of expressive intensity. To quantify the geometric similarity between the frames selected by human observers and those identified by the displacement-based procedure, we reconstructed the 3D facial geometry of each frame using Medusa (Schyns Lab; https://schynslab.github.io/medusa), a Python-based toolbox for dynamic face modeling [45] [46] [47]. For each video stimulus, a three-dimensional tensor of vertex coordinates (3 × 468 × 150) was generated, corresponding to the x, y, and z spatial positions of 468 tracked facial landmarks across 150 frames. For each actor, the human-selected and displacement-based meshes were then compared by computing the root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) between corresponding vertices (see [48] for details). Vertex-wise Euclidean distances were first obtained for all 468 points, squared, averaged, and square-rooted to yield a single RMSD value per pair. This measure reflects the overall magnitude of geometric displacement between the two expressions and provides a standard index of facial shape difference [49] [50]. To allow comparisons across actors with different facial scales, RMSD values were normalized by each actor's full range of facial deformation. Normalized RMSD values were consistently small, well below 1% of the actor's total expressive motion range, indicating that participants' selections closely approximated the apex frames identified by the registration procedure. A visualization of the two overlaid meshes (one obtained from the frame selected by the algorithm and one from the frame identified by human scorers) for each actor is provided in the Supplementary Materials.

For the matched-intensity condition, a two-stage selection process was employed. First, video clips depicting happiness were manually inspected by one of the authors (E.B.) to identify the frame immediately preceding the exposure of teeth. This step sought to minimize potential visual confounds, as exposed teeth may generate a "blob" of increased local contrast and luminance in the mouth region [34]. After identifying happy facial expressions of intermediate intensity, an independent cohort of 11 scorers (7 females, M age = 31 ± 7 years) was recruited to perform an online intensity-matching task. This cohort included all the scorers who participated in the selection of frames with maximum facial displacement and two additional participants. Specifically, they were shown the pre-selected happy facial expression on the left side of the screen, serving as the reference stimulus. On the right side, they could browse a sequence of static frames extracted from the anger video clips of the same actor or actress. These frames were displayed in their original temporal order, progressing from a neutral expression to peak emotional intensity. Using a slider, participants navigated through the entire sequence of the anger expression and were asked to select the frame they perceived as most closely matching the reference happy expression in terms of intensity (see Supplementary Materials, Fig. S1). To familiarize participants with the task logic, a visual analogy was provided: participants were shown a reference blue square and asked to estimate its brightness on a 1-6 scale. Subsequently, they viewed a series of green squares with varying brightness levels and were instructed to identify the one whose brightness most closely resembled that of the blue square. Analogously, participants were asked to treat the happy expression as a reference point along an imagined intensity continuum and to select the corresponding anger frame that best matched this perceived intensity. After all participants completed this intensity-matching task, we calculated the mean frame selection across all participants to identify the matched-intensity angry stimulus for the experiment. This process resulted in the creation of 19 perceptually-equalized stimulus pairs, each consisting of one happy expression and one angry expression for each actor/actress, matched in terms of perceived emotional intensity. These pairs were subsequently presented in the matchedintensity experimental condition.

Notably, all images underwent the same preprocessing pipeline. Non-facial areas (e.g., hair, neck, etc.) were removed by applying a standardized ellipsoidal mask. Images were then resized to equal dimensions, converted to grayscale, and normalized for luminance and spatial frequency using the SHINE toolbox for MATLAB [51], thereby ensuring parity in low-level visual properties across stimuli and conditions.

As a final step, we quantified geometric differences between stimulus pairs to assess how the facial configuration of angry and happy expressions varied across intensity conditions. This analysis served to validate the intensity manipulation, with greater dissimilarity expected in the unmatched-intensity condition (where expressions were presented at maximal, unequalized intensity across emotions) and smaller dissimilarity anticipated in the matched-intensity condition, where expressions were intended to exhibit comparable perceptual distinctiveness. Facial motion data were reconstructed using Medusa and geometric differences were computed using the same RMSD-based approach described above. For each actor, the angry and happy target frames were compared to obtain a single RMSD value reflecting the magnitude of facial shape difference between the two expressions. All RMSD values from the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions were subsequently compared using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test to assess whether intensity equalization significantly reduced the geometric disparity between angry and happy faces.

Experimental procedure

The experiment was conducted online and implemented through jsPsych [52], an opensource JavaScript library specifically designed for precise stimulus presentation and accurate behavioral data acquisition in web-based cognitive tasks. Upon accessing the study link, participants were first presented with a comprehensive overview of the experimental procedures, including detailed information on data confidentiality and security. Only individuals who explicitly provided informed consent were allowed to proceed with the task. Prior to the main experimental task, the short form of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI-SF; [53]), an abbreviated version of the original instrument developed by Oldfield [54], was administered to assess dominant hand preference and account for potential variability in task performance related to handedness. To ensure consistency in stimulus presentation and response modality, participants were instructed to complete the experiment on a laptop or desktop computer.

The task comprised five blocks of 50 trials each, resulting in a total of 250 trials per participant. On each trial, participants were presented with an array of eight grayscale photographs of facial expressions arranged in a circular layout (Fig. 1), with each face having the same eccentricity with respect to a central fixation point. Arrays contained either exclusively neutral faces or a single emotionally-discrepant face (either angry or happy) among neutral distractors. Therefore, the task was articulated into three trial types: (i) neutral arrays with no emotional face (60 trials total, 12 per block); (ii) arrays containing one angry face among neutral distractors (95 trials total, 19 per block); and (iii) arrays containing one happy face among neutral distractors (95 trials total, 19 per block). Randomization was implemented at multiple levels to minimize systematic biases: (i) the sequence of trial types was randomized within each block of 50 trials, and (ii) stimulus location was randomized at the trial level by randomly assigning the actors to the eight possible locations on each trial. However, to control for potential location-based confounds, each emotional expression (angry or happy) of a given actor was consistently assigned to the same location within a block. For example, if an actor's angry expression appeared in Position 3 (e.g., north-east) in a given block, their happy expression was also presented in Position 3 during that block, ensuring that differences in detection accuracy or response times between emotions were not attributable to spatial location.

Participants were instructed to indicate, as quickly and accurately as possible, whether an emotional facial expression was present or absent in the set by pressing designated keys. The online platform was designed to automatically record two primary trial-by-trial metrics throughout the experiment: detection accuracy and speed. Accuracy was defined as the participant's correct identification of the presence/absence of an emotional expression among neutral distractors. Speed was operationalized as reaction time (RT) measured in milliseconds (ms), and refers to the time interval between the presentation of the facial stimulus array on the screen and the participant's keypress response. Participants were required to respond to every trial for the experiment to proceed. The estimated duration of the task was approximately 30 minutes, and compensation was provided at a rate of $8/hour, in accordance with Prolific's recommended payment guidelines.

Upon completing the task, participants were redirected to a debriefing page, which included a completion code to claim their compensation.

Statistical framework and inferential criteria

To overcome limitations of traditional Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), which cannot provide support for the null hypothesis (H 0 ) when results are non-significant, we adopted an interval testing framework. This involves specifying an acceptance region for H 0 and determining whether the observed effect falls within this region (supporting H 0 ) or outside it (supporting the alternative hypothesis, H 1 ). This framework allowed for the formal evaluation of our hypotheses: (1) the presence of a difference in the detection of angry versus happy faces in the unmatched-intensity condition, and (2) the absence of such a difference in the matched-intensity condition.

We preregistered and developed a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification model to assess whether emotion category ("angry" vs. "happy") could be predicted from participants' task performance. Input features included binary accuracy scores (1 = correct,0 = incorrect) and reaction times (RTs), which were normalized for each participant by subtracting the mean reaction time across conditions from individual trials, so as to account for differences in baseline response speed between individuals. The target variable, or the outcome being predicted, was the emotion label associated with each trial. To assess the predictive performance of our model, we employed a nested 5-Fold cross-validation procedure. Thus, the dataset was first divided into five folds for outer cross-validation. In each iteration, one fold was held out as a test set and the remaining four were used for learning. Within each outer learning set, an additional inner 4-fold cross-validation (3 folds iteratively assigned to the training and 1 to the validation sets) was performed to identify the optimal number of neighbors (k) for the k-NN algorithm. A range of k-values was tested, and the optimal k was chosen based on the smallest validation error across the inner folds. The final k-NN model was trained on the entire outer learning set using the optimal k and evaluated on the held-out outer test fold. This procedure was repeated across all outer folds, and classification accuracy (i.e., the proportion of correctly predicted trials) was computed for each one.

Bootstrapping of individual trials in the test set (10,000 resamples) was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals around the classification accuracy estimates.

Decision thresholds for H 0 and H 1 were preregistered before collection of any data and established using a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of 66% accuracy, which we considered practically significant for our analysis. A bootstrapped confidence interval lying entirely above 66% was interpreted as support for H 1 , indicating that the behavioral predictors (speed and accuracy) reliably discriminate between angry and happy expressions. Conversely, an interval entirely below 66% was interpreted as support for H 0 , suggesting that the behavioral features lack sufficient predictive value. Confidence intervals overlapping the 66% threshold were deemed inconclusive.

To quantify the unique contribution of each behavioral predictor (i.e., response accuracy and detection speed) to the classifier's performance, we employed a permutation-based featureimportance analysis embedded within the outer loop of our nested cross-validation procedure.

After selecting the optimal number of neighbors (k) via the inner folds and computing the baseline test accuracy on the held-out data, we permuted the values of one feature within the training data, leaving all other features and the test set unchanged. The classification accuracy of the permuted model was then evaluated on the test set, allowing us to measure the drop in accuracy attributable solely to the disruption of that feature's information. The entire procedure was repeated 100 times per predictor and outer fold, yielding a distribution of permuted accuracies whose average deviation from the baseline provided an estimate of the feature's importance. These scores were averaged across all five outer folds. Large drops in accuracy indicated that the feature carried critical discriminative power, whereas minimal changes revealed a negligible role in distinguishing angry from happy expressions.

Although our primary inferences were based on comparing classification accuracy against a predefined practical threshold (SESOI = 66%) using a frequentist approach, we additionally conducted Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses [55] [56] for each emotion (angry, happy) and condition (matched, unmatched) to evaluate whether the data supported the absence of a practically meaningful advantage when facial displacement was equated across emotions. To this end, we estimated the 95% highest density interval (HDI) of the posterior distribution of population classification accuracy and compared it with a priori ROPE bounds corresponding to negligible effects (i.e., less than "very small"), derived from widely used oddsratio effect-size taxonomies [57] [58] [59] [60]. We specified a uniform prior, Beta(1, 1), and leveraged the conjugacy of the beta distribution for proportions to compute the posterior in closed form.

Specifically, the a parameter was updated with the number of correctly classified trials and the b parameter with the number of misclassified trials. This procedure was repeated for each outer fold of the k-Nearest Neighbors classifier. Given the large number of observations per fold (i.e., thousands of trials), the likelihood was expected to dominate the posterior; consequently, although alternative prior specifications were not formally tested, the results are unlikely to be sensitive to the choice of prior.

Before assessing the k-NN performance in the unmatched-and matched-intensity groups, we verified that the two cohorts were demographically similar, ruling out potential confounds in age, gender, or handedness that might influence task performance. To this end, we conducted several statistical controls. Gender distributions were compared using Fisher's exact test, while group differences in age and laterality quotient (LQ), a continuous index of handedness retrieved from the administration of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, were assessed via two separate Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Also, to examine any gender-handedness interaction, LQs were binned into "left-handers", "ambidextrous", and "right-handers" categories, and gender-by-handedness frequencies cross-tabulated in separate 2×3 tables for each cohort. Chi-squared test was used on each table to determine whether the observed distribution of handedness categories differed by gender more than expected by chance.

To further assess the potential influence of individual differences on classification performance, we conducted an additional non-preregistered k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) analysis in which demographic variables, namely gender, age, and laterality quotient, were incorporated into the feature set alongside behavioral measures of accuracy and response times. Separate models were trained for the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions. This procedure served as a robustness check to ensure that effects attributed to the experimental manipulation were not confounded by heterogeneity in demographics between groups. If classification performance remained stable with the inclusion of these covariates, it would strengthen the interpretation that the observed effects primarily reflect task-related behavioral differences. Feature importance scores were also computed to quantify the relative contributions of demographic and behavioral variables, replicating the analysis framework used for the preregistered analysis. Nevertheless, to further control for inter-individual variability, we conducted a second experiment (Study 2) employing a within-subject design, thereby providing a stringent test of whether classification accuracy reflected stimulus properties rather than participant-level differences.

Beyond these group-level analyses, which involved training classifiers on pooled data across participants, we conducted a complementary non-preregistered single-subject k-NN approach to test whether each individual's behavioral responses could reliably discriminate between emotional expressions. Specifically, we applied k-NN classification separately to each participant's data in both the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions. For each of the 115 participants, trials involving happy and angry target expressions were selected, and a twodimensional feature space was constructed using range-normalized reaction times and binary accuracy values. Within each participant's dataset, 20% of the trials were randomly held out as a test set, while the remaining 80% were partitioned into a training set and a 25% hold-out validation set to determine the optimal number of neighbors (k) by minimizing classification error. The optimal k was then applied to the withheld test set, yielding a single accuracy score per participant.

To estimate the overall classification performance, we generated 10,000 bootstrap resamples of these individual accuracy scores and computed the mean test accuracy along with the corresponding 95% confidence interval for each condition.

In addition to our primary and preregistered k-NN classification and interval testing pipeline, we conducted additional exploratory analyses using Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMMs) to examine the effects of emotion and intensity condition on detection performance, while also accounting for participant-level and stimulus-level variability. Response accuracy was modeled with a binomial distribution and logit link:

The fixed effects in this model included the main effects of emotion (either being presented with an angry or happy face among neutral distractors), experimental condition (unmatched vs. matched intensity), and their interaction, along with random intercepts for participant (participant_id), actor portraying the emotional expression (actor_id), and participant's laterality quotient (lq).

Participant and actor identities were incorporated to control for participant-specific and stimulusspecific baseline variability in performance, respectively. The laterality quotient, derived from the administration of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, was also included as a random effect to model any consistent influence of handedness-related factors on performance. Consistent with our hypotheses, we expected a significant emotion × condition interaction, whereby the detection advantage for happy faces, likely attributable to the visual salience of the smile, would be pronounced in the unmatched-intensity condition and near-zero when expression intensity was perceptually equated across emotions.

For the reaction time analysis, we applied a similar modeling structure, this time leveraging an inverse Gaussian distribution with a log link to accommodate the positively skewed distribution of response times [61]. Only correct trials were included in this model to ensure that reaction times reflected genuine detection speed rather than error-driven responses:

The model included fixed effects for emotion, condition, and their interaction, alongside random intercepts for participant identity, actor, and laterality quotient, mirroring the model testing differences in accuracy between conditions. As with accuracy, we expected a significant emotion × condition interaction, reflecting a detection advantage for happy faces in the unmatched condition compared to the matched condition.

For both GLMMs, statistical significance was assessed using conventional NHST and a threshold of alpha < 0.05.

Results

Visual search performance was assessed using two key behavioral metrics: detection accuracy and response latency, both computed at the trial level across all observations. In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants achieved an overall accuracy of 91% when pooling all trials together (including trials with neutral expressions only). Error analysis revealed that misses accounted for 8.1% of responses, while false alarms constituted 0.9%. When looking at each emotion individually, detection accuracy was on average lower for angry (~81%) than for happy faces (~98%; Figure 2a). Overall performance was lower in the matched-intensity condition, yielding an accuracy of 81.8%, with misses representing the 16.9% of errors and false alarms the 1.3%. In this condition, the accuracy gap between emotions was reduced: angry targets were detected with an accuracy of 77%, and happy expressions with 79% accuracy (Figure 2e).

Detection speed, operationalized as reaction times (RTs), followed a similar trend. In the unmatched-intensity condition, angry targets were accurately detected with an average RT of 1,727 ± 735 milliseconds, whereas happy targets were correctly identified more rapidly, with a mean RT of 1,230 ± 504 milliseconds (Figure 2b). In the matched-intensity condition, detection times increased for both emotion categories, yielding mean RTs of 1,971 ± 875 milliseconds for angry expressions and 1,879 ± 874 milliseconds for happy expressions (Figure 2f).

A k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classifier was trained separately on data from the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions to predict emotion based on reaction times (RTs) and accuracy. In the unmatched-intensity condition, the model achieved an average classification accuracy of 68.4% (Figure 2c). The bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for this estimate ranged from 67.8% to 69.0%, exceeding the 66% threshold pre-defined as the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI). These results indicate that when intensity is not equalized across expressions, behavioral data contain sufficient information to reliably distinguish whether participants detected a happy or an angry face in the crowd. By contrast, the classifier trained on the matched-intensity data yielded an average test accuracy of 53.2%, with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval ranging from 52.5% to 53.8% (Figure 2g; 2i). Notably, the upper bound of this interval falls well below the SESOI threshold of 66%, indicating that, when perceptual features are equalized between emotional expressions, behavioral performance no longer provides practically meaningful information for predicting whether a happy or angry face was detected.

Feature importance investigation revealed that, in the unmatched-intensity condition, detection speed had a substantially greater impact on classification, causing a 9.96% ± 0.15% decrease in model accuracy when permuted (Figure 2d), whereas response accuracy contributed less, with a 1.10% ± 0.45% decrease. In the matched-intensity condition, both features showed diminished importance: RTs led to a 3.24% ± 0.54% drop, and accuracy contributed only 0.79% ± 0.25% (Figure 2h). To verify that these behavioral differences mirrored changes in facial geometry, we examined the structure of facial expressions across conditions. Angry versus happy RMSD was substantially higher in the unmatched-intensity condition (M = 0.55 ± 0.01) than in the matchedintensity condition (M = 0.20 ± 0.18). A Wilcoxon rank-sum test confirmed that this difference was statistically significant, z = 4.21, p < .001, indicating that equalizing expression intensity substantially reduced the geometric disparity between angry and happy faces. Furthermore, we verified that any observed differences between conditions were not confounded by participant characteristics, and thus confirmed that the two cohorts were demographically balanced. Fisher's exact test showed no significant difference in gender distribution between groups (p = .511). Similarly, a Wilcoxon rank-sum test found no significant differences in age (p = .569), and laterality quotient (LQ) was comparable across groups (p = .680).

Chi-square tests yielded no significant association between gender and handedness within either group (unmatched-intensity condition: χ² = .636, p = .727; matched-intensity condition: χ² = 3.476, p = .176).

Additionally, we conducted a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification analysis by incorporating participants' gender, age, and laterality quotient (LQ) into the feature set alongside behavioral measures (i.e., accuracy and response time). Separate models were trained for the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions.

In the unmatched-intensity condition, the inclusion of these additional variables did not significantly affect classification accuracy, which remained at 67.9% (bootstrapped 95% CI: 67.3% -68.6%), comparable to the 68.4% accuracy observed with behavioral features alone.

Similarly, in the matched-intensity condition, the extended model achieved an accuracy of 51.5% (bootstrapped 95% CI: 50.8% -52.2%), supporting H 0 . Feature importance analysis confirmed that in the unmatched-intensity condition, detection speed was the most influential predictor, with a substantial decrease in model accuracy when permuted (10.5% ± 0.47%). Response accuracy had a small effect (1.59% ± 0.28%), while demographic variables, such as age, gender, and laterality quotient, had minimal impact (0.03%, 0.01%, and 0.15%, respectively). In the matched-intensity condition, all predictors contributed less to classification: permutation of RTs led to a 1.37% ± 0.27% drop in accuracy, response accuracy resulted in a 0.42% ± 0.32% decline, and demographic variables again showed negligible influence (0.40%, 0.02%, and 0.27%, respectively). These findings indicate that demographic factors and handedness are irrelevant for classifying detected facial expressions from behavioral performance.

Bayesian posterior estimates were highly consistent across outer folds and ROPE taxonomies (Fig. 3). In the unmatched-intensity condition, fold-wise posterior medians ranged from 0.675 to 0.694. In contrast, in the matched-intensity condition, posterior medians ranged from 0.517 to 0.544, with the 95% HDIs falling entirely below the thresholds for very small effects across all tested taxonomies [57] [58] [59] [60]. Overall, these Bayesian results converged with the preregistered frequentist interval testing framework based on the 66% SESOI, supporting the absence of a practically meaningful effect in the matched-intensity condition. Results from exploratory analyses using Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMMs) confirmed findings of the preregistered k-NN analysis. Indeed, emotional expression, intensity condition, and importantly their interaction significantly explain visual search performance. A GLMM with a binomial distribution and logit link was applied to response accuracy data (41,960 observations in total), with the model including random intercepts for participants (participant_id), stimuli (actor_id), and laterality quotient (lq) in addition to emotional expression, intensity condition and their interaction as fixed effects. The model was estimated in MATLAB using maximum pseudolikelihood and completed without fitting warnings. The loglikelihood and coefficient covariance matrix were finite, indicating numerical stability.

Examination of the estimated random-effects variance-covariance matrix revealed strictly positive variance components (range: 0.005-0.031), and the matrix was positive definite (all eigenvalues > 0), providing no indication of a singular or overparameterized random-effects structure. For the binomial model, dispersion was fixed at 1, and the Pearson χ²/df ratio (φ = 1.05) did not indicate overdispersion.

We observed a significant main effect of emotion, with accuracy higher for happy faces than angry faces (B = 2.461, 95% CI [2.322, 2.599], SE = .071, t = 34.78, p < .001). The main effect of the experimental condition was also significant, indicating lower accuracy in the matchedintensity condition than in the unmatched-intensity condition (B = -.351, 95% CI [-.614, -.088], SE = .134, t = -2.61, p = .009). Notably, the interaction between emotion and condition was also significant (B = -2.353, 95% CI [-2.509, -2.197], SE = .080, t = -29.57, p < .001), suggesting that HSE was markedly diminished when low-level visual features were equalized.

A separate GLMM with an inverse Gaussian distribution and log link function was used to model reaction times (RTs), including the same random-and fixed-effect structure. After excluding incorrect trials, 35,085 observations remained in total. The model was estimated in MATLAB using maximum pseudolikelihood, and completed without fitting warnings. The loglikelihood and coefficient covariance matrix were finite, indicating numerical stability. Inspection of the random-effects variance-covariance matrix revealed positive variance components on the log-transformed RT scale (range: 0.00047-0.00066) and a positive-definite structure (all eigenvalues > 0), suggesting no singular or degenerate random-effects specification.

Fixed effects revealed a significant main effect of emotion: happy faces were detected faster than angry faces (B = -.326, 95% CI [-.337, -.315], SE = .006, t = -57.74, p < .001). There was also a significant main effect of condition, with faster responses overall in the unmatchedintensity condition (B = .128, 95% CI [.077, .178], SE = .026, t = 4.98, p < .001). Again, the interaction between emotion and condition was significant (B = .269, 95% CI [.251, .286], SE = .009, t = 30.44, p < .001), indicating that the speed advantage for happy faces was more pronounced under unmatched intensity.

Study 2

A second preregistered experiment with a within-subject design was conducted to test the replicability of findings obtained in Study 1.

Methods

Experimental design

The present study employed a within-subject design to replicate the effect observed in the preregistered matched-intensity condition from Study 1. To this end, individuals who had previously participated in the unmatched-intensity condition (where angry and happy faces were displayed at their maximum, unequalized intensity) were re-invited to complete the matchedintensity condition. Consistent with the original study protocol, facial expressions in the matchedintensity condition were presented at an intermediate, perceptually-equalized intensity level across emotions. This follow-up was preregistered as an update to the original study registration and is publicly accessible at http://osf.io/sjvak. The conduction of Study 2 was motivated by both theoretical and statistical considerations. Testing for the presence or absence of the HSE within the same participants potentially reduces error variance attributable to inter-individual differences (e.g., perceptual sensitivity, attentional strategies, or baseline emotion detection ability), thereby allowing more robust inferences regarding the role of low-level visual features. Consequently, any observed effects (or lack thereof) can be more confidently attributed to the experimental manipulation (i.e., intensity matching of facial expressions) rather than to uncontrolled betweenparticipant variability. For a visual depiction of the experimental design from both Studies 1 and 2, see the OSF project repository at http://osf.io/vhcyt.

Participants

To replicate the absence of the HSE observed in the matched-intensity condition, individuals who had previously completed the unmatched-intensity condition were re-invited to participate in the follow-up study. Recruitment was conducted using the "Include List" feature on the Prolific platform, which facilitated the precise identification and targeted re-invitation of eligible individuals. Data collection for Study 2 began at least two weeks after the completion of the initial session, allowing for a sufficient washout period to minimize potential carryover effects related to stimuli memorization. All participants received the link to the experiment as in the previous session but were directed to complete the matched-intensity condition task. The order of condition exposure was therefore fixed: all participants first completed the unmatched-intensity task and were subsequently invited to complete the matched-intensity one. The maximum data collection period was set at two weeks; however, data collection could conclude earlier if all eligible participants completed the task before the deadline. Notably, participants received compensation consistent with that of Study 1.

In accordance with the original preregistered protocol, the target sample size for Study 2 was set at 115 participants, each completing 250 trials in the matched-intensity condition (50 trials per block across 5 blocks). As specified in the preregistration update, if fewer than 115 participants completed Study 2, additional participants with no prior involvement in any of our experiments would be recruited. These new participants were asked to complete both the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions in that fixed order, separated by a washout period of at least two weeks. Since the target sample size was not reached within the initial cohort (n = 80), recruitment was extended to include an additional 70 newly enrolled participants, who were asked to take part in both experimental sessions. They first undertook the unmatched-intensity condition and, after a two-week washout period, were recontacted to engage in the matched-intensity condition. Of these, 60 returned for the second session (drop-out rate = ~14%). As the study design required within-participants comparisons, analyses were restricted to those participants who completed both conditions. This resulted in a total of 140 participants (80 from the first wave and 60 from the second) eligible for inclusion. Accordingly, a matched subset of 140 participants was extracted from the unmatched-intensity dataset: specifically, those who also completed the matchedintensity condition. Following this procedure, the final pre-exclusion sample consisted of 140 participants for each condition. Data quality control was then applied following the same exclusion criteria as in Study 1.

No participants were excluded based on completion times below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR). However, participants whose accuracy in either emotion category fell below Q1 -1.5 × IQR were removed to mitigate the influence of random responses, inattentiveness, or misunderstanding of task instructions. This led to the exclusion of 17 participants in the unmatched-intensity condition and 11 in the matched-intensity condition, with overlapping exclusions resulting in a final sample of 115 participants retained for analysis. Therefore, no random subsampling was required and the final sample comprised all eligible participants who completed both sessions and passed exclusion criteria. At the trial level, responses with reaction times exceeding Q3 + 1.5 × IQR were removed, as such latencies may indicate distraction or disengagement. This resulted in the exclusion of 1,098 trials from the unmatchedintensity condition and 1,323 trials from the matched-intensity condition.

Experimental procedure

The experimental procedure for Study 2 largely followed the protocol of Study 1, involving the same visual search task and trial structure. Participants who had previously completed the unmatched-intensity condition were invited to complete the matched-intensity condition only. For participants newly recruited during Study 2, both the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions were administered sequentially, with a washout period of at least two weeks between sessions. Detailed descriptions of the task design, instructions, and stimuli presentation are provided in the Study 1 Methods section.

Replication of the preregistered analytical framework

For Study 2, we replicated the analysis pipeline used in the original preregistered study.

Specifically, the same code and functions uploaded to the OSF project repository prior to the preregistration update were applied to the Study 2 dataset, ensuring consistency in all analyses across studies. This includes variable transformations, inference criteria, data exclusion rules, treatment of missing data, and exploratory analyses.

Facial displacement in relation to visual search performance

A central aim of the present study was to test whether detection performance is better accounted for by perceptual features than by emotional categorization. Therefore, in addition to all previously described analyses, we measured whether participants responded more accurately and faster to faces that are perceptually more distinctive, irrespective of the emotion they depict.

First of all, we quantified the magnitude of facial displacement of angry and happy expressions with respect to a neutral configuration and tested whether larger deviations systematically predicted more accurate and faster responses.

For each stimulus, we computed the root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) between the actor's reconstructed 3D facial mesh of the neutral frame (Frame 1) and that of the frames selected to represent each emotional expression. In the unmatched-intensity condition, the apex frames from angry and happy video sequences were identified through framewise displacement analysis; in the matched-intensity condition, the frames were selected during the intensity-matching task (see Study 1: Stimulus selection and perceptual matching for details). As expected, a Wilcoxon rank-sum test confirmed that RMSD values were significantly greater in the unmatched than in the matched-intensity condition (z = 2.37, p = .018). We then evaluated whether this geometric distance explained response accuracy and RTs at the stimulus level. Data from all experimental designs were pooled and aggregated into actor × emotion × condition units, so that for each unique combination we computed (a) the proportion of correct responses (accuracy) across all emotionaltarget trials and (b) the mean RT across correctly-detected trials, along with the stimulus's corresponding geometric deviation from the neutral baseline. This procedure yielded 76 stimuluslevel observations. The aggregated data were analyzed using two Generalized Linear Mixedeffects Models (GLMMs) predicting detection performance from geometric deviation, condition, and their interaction. In both models, condition was included to reflect systematic differences in deformation magnitude arising from the stimulus-construction procedure, and the interaction term assessed whether the influence of geometric deviation differed between unmatched-and matchedintensity conditions. Emotion was added to determine whether categorical emotion explained variance in accuracy and RTs beyond geometric structure. Actor identity was included as a random intercept to account for between-actor variability: [accuracy OR RTs] ~ geometric distance * condition + emotion + (1|actor_ID)

Results

Visual search performance was assessed using the same behavioral metrics as in Study 1: detection accuracy and response latency. In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants achieved an overall accuracy of ~90% when aggregating trials across emotional categories (including trials with neutral expressions only). Error analysis revealed that misses accounted for 9.1% of responses, while false alarm represented 1.1%. When looking at each emotion individually, angry targets were detected with an average accuracy of ~79%, whereas happy targets were identified with ~97% accuracy. In contrast, overall performance declined in the matchedintensity condition, dropping to 85.3%, with misses representing the 12.9% of errors and false alarms the 1.8%. In this condition, the disparity in detection accuracy between emotional categories was attenuated: angry targets were detected with an accuracy of 84%, and happy expressions with 82% accuracy. Reaction times (RTs) mirrored these patterns. In the unmatchedintensity condition, angry targets were accurately detected with an average RT of 1,769 ± 765 milliseconds, whereas happy targets were correctly identified more rapidly, with a mean RT of 1,278 ± 519 milliseconds. In the matched-intensity condition, detection latencies increased overall, with angry expressions detected at a mean RT of 1,799 ± 809 milliseconds and happy expressions at 1,732 ± 855 milliseconds.

The same k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification procedure used in Study 1 was applied to Study 2, with separate models trained on data from the unmatched-and matchedintensity conditions to predict emotional expression (happy vs. angry) based on participants' reaction times (RTs) and accuracy. In the unmatched-intensity condition, the model achieved an average classification accuracy of 68.7%. The bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for this estimate ranged from 68.1% to 69.3%, exceeding the predefined SESOI of 66%. By contrast, classification performance in the matched-intensity condition yielded an average test accuracy of 53.5%, with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval ranging from 52.8% to 54.2%. Again, the upper bound of this interval fell well below the SESOI threshold of 66%, indicating that behavioral features no longer carried practically meaningful information for emotion prediction when facial expression intensity was equalized. Feature importance analysis showed that, in the unmatchedintensity condition, detection speed had a dominant influence on classification (9.53% ± 0.01% drop in model accuracy when permuted), whereas response accuracy contributed modestly, with a 1.67% ± 0.36% decrease. In the matched-intensity condition, both features were less informative: RTs led to a 3.18% ± 0.42% drop, and accuracy contributed only 1.18% ± 0.37%.

In addition, we conducted a non-preregistered single-subject k-NN classification analysis on data merged from both experimental designs. In the unmatched-intensity condition, the average classification accuracy reached 67.9%, with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval ranging from 66.3% to 69.5%. In contrast, in the matched-intensity condition the average classification accuracy was 54.1%, with a 95% confidence interval of 53.0% to 55.2%. As the entire confidence interval lies above the SESOI in the case of the unmatched-intensity condition and below it in the case of matched-intensity condition, these additional analyses confirm support for the presence (H 1 ) of the HSE when perceptual features are not controlled and its absence (H 0 ) when, instead, perceptual features are equalized.

Consistent with the approach adopted in Study 1, we conducted exploratory analyses using Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMMs) to assess the influence of emotional expression, intensity condition, and their interaction on visual search performance. A GLMM with a binomial distribution and logit link function was applied to response accuracy data (n = 41,951 observations in total). The model included fixed effects for emotion expression, intensity condition, and their interaction, and random intercepts for participants (participant_id), stimuli (actor_id), and laterality quotient (lq). The analysis yielded a significant main effect of emotion, with higher accuracy for happy rather than angry faces (B = 2.410, 95% CI [2.283, 2.538], SE = .065, t = 37.02, p < .001). A significant main effect of the experimental condition was also observed, indicating higher accuracy in the matched-intensity condition compared to the unmatched-intensity condition (B = .409, 95% CI [.333, .484], SE = .039, t = 10.60, p < .001).

Importantly, the interaction between emotion and condition was also significant (B = -2.611, 95% CI [-2.760, -2.461], SE = .076, t = -34.25, p < .001), indicating that the accuracy advantage for happy faces was markedly attenuated when expression intensity was matched.

A separate GLMM with an inverse Gaussian distribution and log link function was estimated to model RTs, employing the same fixed-and random-effects structure as the accuracy model. Following the exclusion of incorrect responses, 35,866 trials were retained in total. The model revealed a significant main effect of emotion, with faster detection of happy faces relative to angry faces (B = -.317, 95% CI [-.329, -.305], SE = .006, t = -51.40, p < .001). In this model, the main effect of intensity condition was not statistically significant (B = -.004, 95% CI [-.017, .010], SE = .007, t = -.53, p = .599). However, the interaction between emotion and condition did reach significance (B = .280, 95% CI [.263, .298], SE = .009, t = 30.92, p < .001), suggesting that the detection speed advantage for happy faces was attenuated under the matched-intensity condition, where perceptual features were equated.

Facial displacement in relation to visual search performance

Detection performance was examined at the stimulus level using Generalized Linear Mixed-effects Models (GLMMs). Separate models were fitted for accuracy and RTs, allowing us to assess whether geometric deviation from the neutral facial configuration predicts detection performance across both outcome measures, and whether this relationship differs between unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions or across emotion categories. The model explained a substantial portion of variance in accuracy (adj R² = ~.35). Geometric distance was a significant positive predictor (B = .739, 95% CI [.288, 1.190], SE = .226, t = 3.26, p = .002), indicating that stimuli that deviated more strongly from the neutral configuration were detected more accurately (Figure 4a). Neither condition (B = .003, 95% CI [-.118, .124], SE = .061, t = .05, p = .958) nor the distance × condition interaction (B = -.014, 95% CI [-.414, .386], SE = .201, t = -.07, p = .945) related to accuracy, and the effect of emotion did not reach significance (B = -.090, 95% CI [-.185, .005], SE = .048, t = -1.89, p = .064). To quantify the contribution of each predictor, we computed the difference between the R² of the full model and that of a reduced model omitting the predictor of interest. Removing geometric distance produced the largest reduction in R² (ΔR² = .17), whereas removing emotion or condition had only a minimal effect (ΔR² < .02).

The model similarly revealed a significant main effect of geometric distance on reaction times (Figure 4b): stimuli that deviated more strongly from the neutral configuration were associated with significantly faster responses (B = -.649, 95% CI [-1.040, -.258], SE = .196, t = -3.31, p = .001). Neither emotion (B = .013, 95% CI [-.072, .097], SE = .043, t = .29, p = .769) nor condition (B = -.044, 95% CI [-.153, .065], SE = .055, t = -.81, p = .423) predicted detection speed, and the interaction between distance and condition did not reach significance (B = -.298, 95% CI [-.643, .048], SE = .173, t = -1.72, p = .090).
