The full model yielded an adjusted R² of .760. Model comparisons showed again that geometric distance contributed the most to model fit (ΔR² = .204), followed by condition (ΔR² = .085), whereas emotion contributed minimally (ΔR 2 < .01).

Although not preregistered, these results indicate that the degree to which a facial expression deviates from its neutral configuration is a reliable predictor of detection performance, whereas the emotional category does not contribute to visual search behavior once geometric deviation is accounted for. Study 3 A third experiment was conducted to test whether the association between a HSE in visual search and lack of equalization of perceptual features of facial expressions also translates into specific patterns of eye gaze.

Methods

Experimental design

The current non-preregistered study employed the same within-subject design as Study 2.

For this in-lab experiment we recruited a convenience sample of 16 participants (8 females; M age = 25 ± 3 years), who completed the standard visual search task involving angry and happy facial expressions across different experimental conditions. As in the original study protocol, stimuli were presented at their respective maximal, yet not equalized, intensity in the unmatched-intensity condition, while displayed at an intermediate, perceptually-equalized intensity level across emotions in the matched-intensity condition. This time, eye movements were continuously recorded throughout the task to capture attentional deployment.

Besides previously employed behavioral measures, eye-tracking indices, namely Time To First Fixation (TTFF; the latency between the onset of a visual stimulus and the moment a participant first fixates on an area of interest, or AOI), and dwell time (total time spent on a particular AOI), were also analyzed to examine the spatiotemporal allocation of attention across experimental conditions and emotional categories. In line with previous behavioral findings, the unmatched-intensity condition was expected to favor happy targets in two respects: (1) attracting the first fixation earlier, and (2) eliciting shorter dwell times. Both outcomes would indicate a more efficient visual search, reflecting an attentional bias toward perceptually conspicuous features, such as a broad, tooth-exposing smile, which enhance contrast and perceptual distinctiveness. Conversely, in the matched-intensity condition, where facial displacement is equalized and prominent local features are minimized, asymmetries in TTFF and dwell time were expected to be attenuated, indicating that the putative HSE is not specific to emotional category per se, but rather contingent on the perceptual characteristics of facial expressions that guide early attention in visual search [22, 34].

Participants

Participants were adult Italian volunteers, recruited through local university channels and word-of-mouth. An initial screening phase was conducted to exclude individuals with any visual impairments, neurological/psychiatric conditions and those taking medications that could potentially affect task performance. After receiving a detailed explanation of the experimental procedures, all eligible participants provided written informed consent to take part in the study. The final sample consisted of 15 participants, following the exclusion of one individual due to technical issues.

Stimuli

The same dataset of stimuli used in Studies 1 and 2 was also employed in the present experiment. As in Study 1, participants were asked to perform an intensity-matching task through the designated web interface (see Fig. S1 in Supplementary Materials). They were shown a preselected happy facial expression (characterized by a subtle smile with no visible teeth) on the left side of the screen, which served as the reference stimulus. On the right side, they could browse a sequence of static frames extracted from anger video clips of the same actor or actress, displayed in their original temporal order, typically progressing from a neutral expression to peak intensity.

Using a slider, participants navigated through the entire sequence of the anger expression and selected the frame they perceived as most closely matching the reference happy expression in terms of expressive intensity. Unlike in Study 1, where the average frame selection across participants was calculated to derive a single matched-intensity stimulus for each actor, in the current study the selected frames were retained individually. This means that the experimental stimuli were created ad hoc for each participant, based on their personal judgments of expressive intensity.

For the unmatched-intensity condition, video clips of happy and angry expressions were processed as in the previous experiments, through frame-by-frame analysis to identify the one with the highest displacement values. Finally, all stimuli underwent the same aforementioned preprocessing pipeline before presentation in the visual search task (i.e., elliptical cropping, conversion to grayscale, equalization of luminance and spatial frequency).

Experimental procedure

The experiment was conducted in a soundproof environment under controlled light conditions. Stimuli were presented on a 32-inch Display++ calibrated monitor (Cambridge Research Systems), with a resolution of 1920x1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 120 Hz. Stimulus presentation and data collection were implemented in MATLAB using Psychtoolbox 3.0.17. The task comprised five blocks of 40 trials each, resulting in a total of 200 trials per participant.

Consistent with the previous visual search task, each trial displayed eight facial-expression photographs arranged in a circular configuration around a central white fixation cross against a gray background (see Figure 1). Each picture subtended a visual angle of 7.3° x 5.0° on the screen when viewed from a distance of 68 cm. To reduce visual noise, a Gaussian smoothing filter (σ = 1.5) was applied to all facial stimuli. Overall, the task included three trial types: (i) neutral arrays with no emotional face (40 trials total, 8 per block); (ii) arrays containing one angry face among neutral distractors (80 trials total, 16 per block); and (iii) arrays containing one happy face among neutral distractors (80 trials total, 16 per block). Trial types and spatial arrangements were randomized within each block. To control for location-based confounds, however, each actor's angry and happy expressions were consistently presented in the same position within a block (e.g., if an actor's angry face appeared in the top-right position, their happy face was also presented in that position).

Prior to the experimental task, participants completed the short form of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI-SF; [53]) to assess their dominant hand preference. During the task, they were instructed to indicate whether all faces displayed neutral expressions or whether one emotionally discrepant face (angry or happy) was present among distractors. Only two response keys were activated on the keypad, and to minimize potential effects of handedness on response speed, the assignment of keys was counterbalanced across sessions. As soon as a response key was pressed, reaction time was stored, and the fixation mark reappeared. Eye movements were continuously recorded through a table-mounted eye-tracking device (LiveTrack Lightning system, CRS Ltd., Kent, United Kingdom), with a sampling rate of 500 Hz, an accuracy of 0.25° and a resolution of less than 0.05°. A combined forehead and chin rest was used to stabilize head position and maintain a constant viewing distance of 68 cm. Before each session, a calibration phase was performed to ensure the accuracy of eye-tracking measurements. All participants were given a practice session of five trials to familiarize them with the procedure before starting the experiment. Overall, each participant completed 200 trials (40 trials per 5 blocks), of which 80% contained one discrepant target and 20% did not.

Oculomotor analyses

As concerns eye-tracking measures, we adopted a time-course decomposition of manual response latencies into three sequential epochs: (1) initiation time, defined as the latency from stimulus onset to the first saccade, (2) scanning time, defined as the interval from the first saccade onset to the first fixation within the target area of interest (AOI) and ( 3) verification time, defined as the interval from the first fixation within the target AOI to the manual response [62]. The initiation and scanning epochs together capture the time required to orient attention and visually search the array of neutral distractors to locate the target. Target AOIs were defined around the emotionally-discrepant face in each trial (see Figure 5). Verification time reflects the subsequent evaluation of the target stimulus as relevant for the task. In the present experiment, these epochs were estimated directly from valid gaze-position samples: initiation time was operationalized as the latency to the first gaze sample outside the central fixation area; scanning time as the interval from this departure to the first sample within the target AOI; and verification time as the interval from the first AOI entry to the participant's button press. TTFF was computed as the sum of the initiation and scanning epochs, with the first entry into the target-face AOI serving as a samplebased approximation of the first fixation [22, 63].

Dwell time was defined as the cumulative period during which the gaze remained within a predefined AOI, calculated by summing the time intervals between consecutive valid gaze samples within that region. For each trial, dwell times were computed for the target face as a whole, as well as separately for the eyes and mouth regions, given their critical role in decoding emotional expressions [41, [64] [65] [66]. The target face AOI was defined as an elliptical region, whereas the eyes and mouth AOIs were defined as rectangular and elliptical regions, respectively. The eyes and mouth AOIs were matched for area (7,332 pixels²), with their dimensions kept constant across stimuli and their positions manually adjusted where necessary to align with the corresponding facial features. A gaze sample was considered within an AOI when the participant's gaze of either eye fell inside its boundaries.

Raw eye-tracking data underwent the following preprocessing pipeline: gaze coordinates falling outside the display boundaries were excluded; trials with incorrect responses or containing only neutral faces were also removed, ensuring that analyses focused exclusively on correctly identified emotional targets. All subsequent analyses were conducted on this cleaned dataset.

Following the same machine-learning framework adopted in the previous studies, we implemented a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification model to predict the emotion category ("angry" vs. "happy") from visual behavior, separately for the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions. Input eye-tracking features were aggregated at the trial level and included TTFF and dwell times on the whole target face, as well as on the eye and mouth AOIs, and verification times.

All predictors were mean-centered within participants to remove individual differences.

Classification accuracy was evaluated as before using a nested 5-fold cross-validation procedure and computed for each outer fold and averaged across folds. Uncertainty around estimates was assessed via bootstrapping of test-set trials (10,000 resamples) to derive a 95% confidence interval.

In line with the behavioral analyses, inferential decisions were based on interval testing using a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of 66% accuracy. Confidence intervals entirely above this threshold were interpreted as evidence for reliable discrimination between angry and happy expressions (supporting H 1 ), whereas intervals entirely below the threshold supported H 0 ; intervals overlapping the threshold were deemed inconclusive. Feature importance was quantified using permutation testing embedded within the outer cross-validation loop. The resulting decrease in classification accuracy, averaged across 100 permutations per feature, was taken as an index of its contribution to emotion decoding. Linear mixed-effects models were also used to examine both the temporal dynamics and the spatial allocation of visual attention to emotionally-discrepant faces. Time To First Fixation (TTFF) and dwell time served as dependent variables in separate models. Fixed effects included emotion (angry vs. happy) and condition (unmatched vs. matched intensity), as well as their interaction. Random intercepts for participants (participant_id) and actors (actor_id) were also included to account for baseline variability across individuals and stimuli:

[TTFF OR Dwell time] ~ emotion * condition + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | actor_id)

To examine the allocation of first fixations to specific facial features, we also analyzed participants' TTFF on the eyes and mouth AOIs. Specifically, we computed a binary variable indicating which AOI was fixated first: 0 for eyes and 1 for mouth. This variable was modeled using a Generalized Linear Mixed-effects Model (GLMM) with a binomial distribution and logit link, including fixed effects of emotion, condition, their interaction, and TTFF on the whole face as a covariate, as well as random intercepts for participants and facial stimuli. Trials in which participants did not fixate either AOI were removed, while trials with missing values for one AOI were assigned according to the available fixation (i.e., if eyes were not fixated, the first fixation was coded as mouth, and vice versa).

Results

Visual search performance was evaluated using the same behavioral indices employed in Studies 1 and 2, namely detection accuracy and response latency. Of the 3,000 trials collected, 600 contained only neutral faces and were excluded from emotion-specific analyses. Accuracy was calculated across the remaining 2,400 emotional-target trials, whereas reaction times were analyzed using the 2,233 trials with correct responses, following the exclusion of 167 incorrect trials. In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants detected angry targets with an average accuracy of ~97%, and happy targets with ~98%. In contrast, overall accuracy decreased in the matched-intensity condition, with angry and happy targets detected at ~86% and ~91%, respectively. Response latencies in the unmatched-intensity condition revealed that angry targets were accurately detected with an average RT of 2,453 ± 2,064 milliseconds, whereas happy targets were correctly identified more rapidly, with a mean RT of 1,441 ± 1,129 milliseconds. In the matched-intensity condition, detection latencies increased across both emotion categories, with angry expressions detected at a mean RT of 2,741 ± 2,078 milliseconds and happy expressions at 2,992 ± 2,670 milliseconds.

Eye-tracking analyses were further restricted to 2,182 trials, following the exclusion of 51 trials in which no gaze entry was observed in either the eyes or mouth AOI. Total manual response latencies were decomposed into initiation time (stimulus onset to first saccade), scanning time (first saccade to first fixation within the target AOI), and verification time (first fixation in the target AOI to manual response). Table 1 reports the descriptive statistics for each epoch. In the unmatched-intensity condition, initiation times were similar for angry (M = 0.34s ± 0.22s) and happy faces (M = 0.34s ± 0.22s), whereas scanning times (angry: M = 0.67s ± 0.67s; happy: M = 0.30s ± 0.45s) and verification times (angry: M = 1.46s ± 1.88s; happy: M = 0.82s ± 0.95s) were shorter for happy faces. In the matched-intensity condition, initiation times again did not substantially differ (angry: M = 0.34s ± 0.18s; happy: M = 0.34s ± 0.17s), while scanning times (angry: M = 0.90s ± 0.89s; happy: M = 0.68s ± 0.72s) and verification times (angry: M = 1.52s ± 1.77s; happy: M = 2.01s ± 2.46s) became comparable across emotions.

Dwell times for the target face were longer for angry (M = 0.84s ± 0.90s) than for happy faces (M = 0.53s ± 0.50s) in the unmatched-intensity condition, while in the matched-intensity condition times were substantially similar for angry (M = 0.86s ± 0.78s) and happy faces (M = 0.94s ± 0.92s). Dwell times for eyes and mouth AOIs are also reported, representing the average time per trial that participants' gaze remained within each AOI. For the eyes AOI, in the unmatched-intensity condition participants spent more time looking at the eyes when viewing angry faces (M = 0.49s ± 0.61s) compared with happy faces (M = 0.20s ± 0.32s). In the matchedintensity condition, dwell times on the eyes were more similar for angry (M = 0.53s ± 0.55s) and happy faces (M = 0.44s ± 0.54s). For the mouth AOI, dwell times were similarly short for angry (M = 0.19s ± 0.34s) and happy faces (M = 0.22s ± 0.30s) in the unmatched-intensity condition, whereas in the matched-intensity condition participants spent more time looking at the mouth when viewing happy faces (M = 0.32s ± 0.44s) than angry faces (M = 0.16s ± 0.33s).

Temporal epochs and dwell times for angry and happy faces across intensity conditions. Mean ± standard deviation (SD) of initiation, scanning, and verification times in seconds, as well as dwell times on the target face, eyes and mouth AOIs, are reported separately for angry and happy expressions in the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions. N indicates the number of trials included in each condition, for a total of 2,182 trials from 15 participants. Consistent with Studies 1 and 2, a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classifier was trained separately on eye-tracking data from the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions to predict emotion category. In the unmatched-intensity condition, the model achieved an average classification accuracy of 70.3%, with a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval of [67.7% -73.1%], exceeding the pre-defined smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) threshold of 66%. In contrast, classification accuracy in the matched-intensity condition was 56.1%, with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval ranging from 53.1% to 59.1%. The upper bound of this interval fell below the SESOI threshold of 66%, indicating that eye-tracking measures in this case did not yield practically meaningful information for emotion discrimination when perceptual intensity was equalized.

Feature importance investigation showed modest effects for individual predictors in both conditions, but the joint permutation of TTFF on the face and mouth AOIs contributed most to classification performance in the unmatched-intensity condition, resulting in an average accuracy decrease of 2.96% ± 0.89%. By contrast, in the matched-intensity condition, the joint contribution of dwell times on the eyes and mouth regions accounted for the largest reduction in classification accuracy (1.84% ± 1.01%).

A Linear mixed-effects model was also fitted to examine Time To First Fixation (TTFF) as a function of emotion and experimental condition, with TTFF defined as the sum of initiation and scanning times. Results revealed significant main effects of emotion and condition, as well as a significant interaction between them. TTFF was significantly shorter for happy compared with angry faces (B = -.376, 95% CI [-.458, -.294], SE = .042, t = -9.00, p < .001) and longer in the matched-intensity condition compared to the unmatched-intensity one (B = .245, 95% CI [.160, .330], SE = .044, t = 5.63, p < .001). The significant interaction (B = .142, 95% CI [.023, .261], SE = .061, t = 2.34, p = .019) indicates that the TTFF advantage for happy versus angry faces was selectively more pronounced in the unmatched-intensity condition, where the physical properties of broad, teeth-exposing smiles amplify the attentional prioritization of happy facial expressions, and attenuated once the perceptual distinctiveness of facial expressions was equalized in the matched-intensity condition.

Dwell time on the target face was analyzed using the same fixed-and random-effects structure. In the unmatched-intensity condition, happy faces received significantly shorter dwell times than angry faces (B = -.315, 95% CI [-.397, -.233], SE = .042, t = -7.54, p < .001). This advantage was significantly attenuated after intensity matching, as indicated by the emotion × condition interaction (B = .380, 95% CI [.261, .499], SE = .061, t = 6.27, p < .001). In the matchedintensity condition, the estimated difference was in the opposite direction and was not statistically significant (happy minus angry: B = .065, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.151], SE = 0.044, t = 1.48, p = .140).

For angry faces, dwell time did not differ significantly between intensity conditions (B = .045, 95% CI [-.040, .131], SE = .044, t = 1.04, p = .299).

A GLMM predicting which facial-feature AOI was entered first (0 = eyes,1 = mouth) revealed that, in the unmatched-intensity condition, happy faces were more likely than angry faces to receive the first gaze entry on the mouth rather than the eyes (B = .461, 95% CI [.213, .709], SE = .126, t = 3.65, p < .001). This difference was significantly attenuated in the matched-intensity condition, as indicated by the emotion × condition interaction (B = -.447, 95% CI [-.804, -.090], SE = .182, t = -2.46, p = .014). No significant main effect of condition was observed (B = .057, 95% CI [-.204, .318], SE = .133, t = .43, p = .668). Longer latencies to first entry into the target face were associated with a lower likelihood of entering the mouth before the eyes (B = -.238, 95% CI [-.373, -.104], SE = .069, t = -3.47, p < .001).

Discussion

Across three studies, we provide converging evidence that emotion-specific advantages in facial expression detection depend strongly on the perceptual characteristics of the stimuli, rather than on their communicative or affective content. In two large behavioral experiments, a detection advantage for happy faces emerged only when expressions were presented at full, perceptually unbalanced intensity. Under these conditions, happy targets were detected more quickly and accurately, and behavioral measures reliably predicted emotion category -replicating prior reports of an apparent HSE with full-intensity photographic expressions (e.g., [20] [21] 34]). Crucially, when expression intensity and facial displacement were matched across emotions, this advantage disappeared, and behavioral performance no longer supported practically meaningful emotion decoding. The same pattern of results was observed across both the preregistered frequentist interval testing framework and a complementary Bayesian analysis, indicating that these conclusions are robust to the inferential framework adopted. A within-subject replication confirmed that this pattern reflected perceptual equalization rather than interindividual differences, consistent with feature-based accounts of visual search [67] [68] [69]. More specifically, our findings converge with previous research demonstrating that the perceptual features of facial expressions strongly influence anger and happiness superiority effects in visual search [24-25, 30, 34, 70].

Eye-tracking data supported the same interpretation. When perceptual differences between expressions were more pronounced, happy targets attracted earlier fixations and shorter dwell times, consistent with more efficient target localization and subsequent processing of prominent facial features such as the smile [34, 71]. Further supporting this interpretation, Stuit and colleagues [72] demonstrated that spatial-frequency information and local edge orientations, particularly around the mouth and cheeks, predicted initial eye movements between faces more accurately than emotional category. Notably, these visual features remained predictive even when the competing faces displayed the same emotion. The perceptual distinctiveness conferred by these features may facilitate target localization not only through attentional guidance toward happy faces, but also through reduced target-distractor similarity, which makes happy targets easier to distinguish from surrounding neutral faces [73]. Indeed, previous eye-tracking studies have shown that the efficiency of visual search is strongly influenced by distractor dwelling, skipping, and revisiting [74] [75], with faster distractor rejection also contributing to happiness superiority [76].

Extending this evidence, Stuit and coauthors [70] examined the respective roles of distractor processing and target identification in this advantage. They found that happy targets were identified more rapidly once fixated, even when either happiness or anger could serve as the target.

In contrast, shorter fixation times on distractors were observed only when participants specifically searched for happy faces.

Beyond the influence of search goals, our findings show that the detection advantage strongly depends on the perceptual differences between emotional expressions. Indeed, when expression intensity was matched, attentional dynamics no longer distinguished facial expressions based on emotion categories. Importantly, detection performance scaled systematically with geometric deviation from a neutral facial configuration: mixed-effects models showed that geometric deformation was the strongest predictor of both accuracy and response speed, accounting for substantially more variance than emotion category or condition. This finding aligns with work demonstrating that exaggerating shape differences from a neutral reference enhances perceptual distinctiveness and recognition [77] [78], and with studies of dynamic expressions showing that detection advantages, particularly for smiles, are driven by morphological and temporal properties of facial motion [79] [80]. Together with evidence that features such as smile configuration, temporal unfolding, and teeth visibility modulate detectability [30, 81], our results = 4.72; [33]), happy expressions were nonetheless perceived as more arousing than angry ones.

Reanalyses by Lundqvist and colleagues [90] further show that whether a happiness-or angersuperiority effect emerges depends largely on the relative arousal of the stimuli, rather than on valence or emotion category alone. Crucially, perceived arousal closely tracks the magnitude of facial deformation: expressions that deviate more strongly from a neutral configuration are judged as more arousing [48]. Such geometric deviations co-occur with visually salient perceptual cues, including increased mouth aperture, teeth exposure, and eye opening, which have been shown to enhance perceptual distinctiveness and facilitate detection [30, 77, 91]. This raises the possibility that perceived arousal is partly inferred from the same physical features that facilitate detection.

Consistent with this account, our mixed-effects analyses identified geometric deviation from neutrality as the strongest predictor of detection performance. When expression intensity was equated across emotions, thereby plausibly minimizing arousal-linked physical differences, no expression retained a detection advantage. A proposed explanation for the HSE emphasizes the high prevalence of happy expressions in everyday social interactions, which may tune the visual system toward more efficient detection of this expression through experience-dependent mechanisms [92] [93]. However, the elimination of this advantage after matching facial displacement between happy and angry expressions indicates that any contribution of exposure is secondary to the perceptual characteristics of stimuli.

Thus, although our findings do not rule out a role for familiarity or learning in face processing more broadly, they suggest that such factors cannot account for detection advantages once perceptual structure is controlled. Future work will be needed to determine the conditions under which experience-based effects contribute independently of the visual properties of facial expressions.

Limitations should be acknowledged. First, behavioral data in Studies 1 and 2 were collected online. Although we applied stringent exclusion criteria, preprocessing procedures, and robustness checks, online testing inevitably introduces additional variability related to display characteristics, viewing conditions, and participant environments that is minimized in laboratory settings. A further concern is the potential inclusion of AI-generated responses, an issue of growing relevance in web-based behavioral research. We did not implement explicit procedures to detect such cases in Studies 1 and 2; however, this is unlikely to have materially affected the data. Unlike questionnaire-based paradigms, where responses can be produced without engaging with perceptual input, the current task required continuous visual processing and rapid responses on a trial-by-trial basis, relying on the coordinated operation of perceptual encoding, attentional selection, and motor execution. At the same time, all responses were constrained to fall within time windows characteristic of human behavior, as our preprocessing pipeline explicitly targeted implausible response patterns by excluding trials and participants with atypical reaction times or performance profiles. Taken together, these considerations make it unlikely that the data were generated by automated systems.

Second, the relatively small in-lab sample (n = 15) in Study 3 reduced the precision of the estimated effects, as reflected in the larger confidence intervals; however, the observed patterns remained consistent with the behavioral findings.

Third, the generalizability of our findings may be limited by the specific task, stimuli, and populations examined. We focused exclusively on happy and angry facial expressions, using static grayscale images in a visual search paradigm. Whether the same perceptual account extends to other emotional expressions, alternative stimulus formats (e.g., color images or fully dynamic faces), or tasks emphasizing recognition rather than detection remains to be established. Furthermore, participants were recruited online from the United States and the United Kingdom in Studies 1 and 2, and from Italy in Study 3, potentially limiting generalizability across cultural contexts.

In conclusion, the present findings indicate that apparent advantages in detecting specific facial expressions are driven by the perceptual characteristics of the stimuli, including expressionrelated features and geometric differences, rather than by the affective information those expressions convey. Without adequate control of these properties, observed detection advantages may be easily misattributed to emotional content, encouraging evolutionary or functional interpretations that may be unwarranted. Our results instead support a parsimonious account grounded in domain-general perceptual mechanisms that do not require an intrinsic attentional preference for specific emotion categories. Systematic variation in the physical features of facial expressions may help explain the inconsistent and often contradictory findings that have characterized decades of research on emotional face detection. Because insufficient control of expression intensity and stimulus appearance remains common in widely used face databases and experimental paradigms, claims of emotion-specific detection advantages should be interpreted with caution. Rigorous control and explicit assessment of perceptual structure are therefore essential for advancing a theoretically coherent understanding of how facial expressions are processed in the visual system. were presented with arrays of eight photographs of actors arranged in a circle around a central fixation cross. reconcile longstanding inconsistencies in the emotional face detection literature and place principled constraints on emotion-centric accounts of attentional prioritization.

Basic emotion theories propose that certain emotions enjoy privileged access to attention because of their evolutionary significance (e.g., [82] [83] [84] [85]). Support for this view has often been drawn from visual search studies reporting enhanced detection of threat-related stimuli [10, [12] [13]. However, attributing such advantages to intrinsic attentional prioritization requires considering the physical characteristics of the stimuli. Our findings show that prioritization was contingent on these characteristics and disappeared when expression intensity and facial displacement were equated. This pattern indicates that apparent emotion-specific prioritization may instead arise from perceptual properties of facial expressions that covary with emotion category, without necessarily invoking specialized, biologically dedicated emotion-processing mechanisms. This interpretation does not call into question the broader observation that affective stimuli can receive attentional priority over neutral stimuli; it challenges the assumption that the relative prioritization of one emotional expression over another necessarily reflects its affective meaning. Converging evidence from a visual-awareness paradigm showed that image contrast features predicted which face reached awareness first, whereas emotional category did not.

Importantly, the visual features predicting perceptual prioritization were not significantly associated with those distinguishing emotional expressions [86]. More broadly, these results are consistent with constructivist and contextual accounts of emotion perception, which emphasize the integration of perceptual features, context, and prior knowledge over the readout of fixed emotion categories [87] [88] [89].

Differences in attentional prioritization may also be explained by variation in stimulus arousal rather than by emotion category per se [90].
